events.title: Iran war energy price shock large but contained so far, IMF chief says
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund has said the energy price shock driven by the US- Iran war has so far been “large but contained”, but warned that energy demand could lead to further pressure. “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. This year's gathering, held in Bangkok, comes as supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East pile on to inflationary pressures, potentially leading to higher interest rates for advanced economies. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank have already begun to raise their key rates, with the Bank of England expected to join them next month. Higher energy prices and rising debt levels have also driven global borrowing costs to their highest levels in decades. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, traded at 5.307 per cent as recently on Monday, its highest level since 2002. That pressure has also spread to markets in other advanced economies including in Japan, France, Germany and the UK. Oil producers in the Middle East are racing to establish alternative routes to bring their exports to the markets. The UAE is fast-tracking construction of its West-East Pipeline , which is expected to double export capacity through Fujairah by the time its expansion is completed in 2027. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude through the East-West Pipeline . The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship tracking firm Kpler. The latest figures included transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Ms Georgieva had credited the Gulf Co-operation Council's efforts to reroute energy supplies for preventing a larger shock to the global economy during a meeting with the bloc's finance ministers and central bankers in Bahrain last week. She also said the IMF anticipates the GCC economy will contract this year, adding that the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping. A separate report from the World Bank released on Tuesday said GCC economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. Meanwhile, continued supply disruptions in liquefied natural gas will hit buyers in Europe and Asia particularly hard, Ms Georgieva said, noting price pressures could further build with winter approaching and reserves dwindling. AI revolution is here In her address, the IMF chief also used her address to urge governments to embark on policies to unlock the productive gains under artificial intelligence . Ms Georgieva described the global economy as one being pulled in two directions, with the positive demand shock from AI partially offsetting the economic fallout from the US-Iran conflict. “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva In the US, the AI buildout is shaping up to become the largest investment drive in the country's history. Analysts at Brookings anticipate AI investment in data centres, infrastructure, chips and other equipment will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, or an average of 3.63 per cent of US GDP per year. The broad S&P 500 hit a fresh record-high of 7,800 on Tuesday driven by renewed AI enthusiasm. But with fears of an AI bubble also fomenting, Ms Georgieva said countries should adopt regulation and supervision as a “first line of defence” to prevent a far-reaching shock if AI earnings fall short. The Trump administration has recently adopted a defensive posture of AI amid a growing domestic backlash against the data centre buildout ahead of November’s midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has taken a light regulatory touch on AI advancement and repeatedly expressed his desire to beat China in the global AI race. Countries in the Gulf are seeking to advance large-scale acceleration of AI. The UAE targets to have AI contribute 20 per cent of its non-oil GDP by 2031. Ms Georgieva said AI could deliver up to a half percentage point of additional world growth – or “adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy” – annually. “Yet as this drives forward today’s AI economies, it largely bypasses most others, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she said.

events.title: Why parents need to be involved in the money conversation with their children
events.summary: (From left) Najwa Chua Ai Xin, UOB Heartbeat volunteer Ho Ying Ying and ST reporter Chor Khieng Yuit searching for frozen food on Najwa's grocery list during a July 22 shopping run. Shopping with real money helps children learn budgeting and financial decision-making through practical experience, as shown by a Primary 6 student managing a $50 budget effectively. Interactive activities like Curiosity Cove provide financial lessons but require parental involvement to make the learning meaningful and encourage discussions on needs versus wants. Digital tools like the Smart Buddy app help parents monitor children’s spending and foster daily conversations about money habits, enhancing financial literacy at home. SINGAPORE – Shopping with real money helps children become more financially savvy. This thought crossed my mind while volunteering on a shopping trip with UOB Heartbeat volunteers on July 22. I was paired with UOB’s Ho Ying Ying and Najwa Chua, 12, who has participated in these outings since she was eight. We began by reviewing the shopping list that Najwa had put together with her parents, before taking a short walk to FairPrice at Rivervale Plaza. Najwa went about getting the items on her list: bananas, grapes, 30 eggs, chicken and bread. Since the chicken was on sale, she picked up two packets. After all, her family loves curry chicken. However, she had to forgo her favourite Lay’s sour cream potato chips because they did not fit her budget. Instead, she opted for two packets of FairPrice house-brand chips, which were on sale. Najwa tried to keep a running tab in her head, but got overwhelmed as her shopping basket filled up, and she asked to borrow Ho’s phone to check the final sum. Her careful budgeting left her enough to buy a bottle of Thai sweet chilli sauce that her parents love. Her final bill came to $49.98, within the $50 she was allocated. It was clear that Najwa actively looked out for deals and knew which brands offered more bang for her buck. She shared that she had picked up budgeting skills and practical tips from the volunteers during previous shopping stints. A spokesperson from Children’s Wishing Well, the charity leading this financial literacy initiative, said that these hands-on experiences and interactions with the volunteers have helped Najwa become more confident in making spending decisions. Today, she knows how to manage her money and adapt her choices to stay within her budget – and not just on these organised shopping runs. Her mother has even entrusted her with the family’s weekly provisions, allowing her to head to the supermarket after school to buy the items on her own. Najwa Chua Ai Xin and her father Chua Peng Huat with her grocery purchases and receipt. Hearing how much Najwa has grown, I thought: “Why not try this out on my daughter?” She is in Primary 2 and will turn eight later in 2026. I started by increasing her daily allowance for school meals to $5, which she can use for both her morning snack and lunch. The experiment is still a work in progress. While her school has taught her about needs and wants, she still tries to justify her wants as a need. Once, she spent $2.50 at the bookshop on a mechanical pencil and pencil leads. When I asked why she bought them when she had normal pencils, she replied, “I need the mechanical pencil to write.” My daughter chose to spend on her perceived “need”. With only $2.50 left for the day, she spent $1.80 on two cheese sticks for her morning snack and decided to skip lunch – which to me is a “need”. Hoping to drive home the “needs versus wants” lesson through play, my husband and I decided to take our daughter to explore Curiosity Cove. During our visit, my husband observed that the financial literacy elements at Curiosity Cove are more of a sideline, and the educational concepts are relegated to “secondary amusement” for the children after they finish playing. Venturing outside Curiosity Cove, we spotted some activity stations around the Mandai area. One station focusing on needs and wants required children to build a virtual buggy. To do so, they had to decide which car parts they needed to buy and which parts they could skip. At the Super Savers Trail at Curiosity Cove, one of the outdoor stations taught children about needs versus wants. Another station touched on savings and interest. By shifting a marker on a slider board, children can see how interest grows as their savings increase – so the more they save, the more they earn. However, these displays would not automatically spur any meaningful discussion or learning unless parents step in to talk about the concepts, using the posters to convey the financial lessons to their children. A simple visualisation of how interest grows as children save more. Banks are offering digital tools to keep that dialogue going. Nelson Neo, DBS’ head of retail banking and head of POSB, noted that the Smart Buddy app enables parents to keep tabs on their children’s spending.

events.title: Woolworths freight fuel levy surcharge almost triples since Iran war
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Consumers to face possible check-out pain as Woolworths increases freight fuel levy surcharge Woolworths has increased its freight fuel levy again amid high diesel costs. ( Supplied: Woolworths ) Woolworths has increased the fuel levy charged through its logistics network to food and grocery suppliers to almost triple its pre-Iran war level as diesel costs continue to climb. The fuel levy surcharges have increased for metro and regional areas, affecting some of the country's largest food and grocery manufacturers. This includes Primary Connect, Woolworths' logistics arm, which transports goods from suppliers to distribution centres and stores across the country. The business manages freight for more than 1,000 grocery producers, including brands such as Sanitarium, PepsiCo, Ingham's and Arnott's. The fuel levy for metro areas recently rose from 17.47 per cent to 19.88 per cent. In regional Australia, the levy increased from 44.20 per cent to 50.30 per cent. University of Sydney supply chain management professor Rico Merkert said the increases were not unusual when diesel prices rose sharply. "Fuel levies are commonly used in freight markets to manage fuel-price volatility," Professor Merkert said. "Many transport operators use surcharges that can be adjusted periodically rather than renegotiating contracts every time fuel costs move. "If diesel costs rise sharply, it is economically reasonable for freight providers and retailers to increase fuel surcharges to recover those additional operating costs." Rico Merkert says transport costs are only one component of the final retail price at the supermarket. ( Supplied ) Prior to the Iran war, the fuel levy Woolworths charged in metro areas was 7.28 per cent. Within weeks of the war, it had risen to 12.47 per cent. The regional fuel levy has jumped by more than 172 per cent since March, when it was 18.44 per cent. "We operate a large distribution network that includes independently owned and operated transport providers, and we are committed to supporting our transport partners, just as other industry players are doing," a Woolworths spokesperson said. "To ensure they can keep their trucks on the road and get products on shelves in stores, we increased our review of the fuel levy to twice monthly in March to reflect the challenges they still face." Experts believe the increase in freight costs are likely to be shared across the supply chain. "My prediction is that consumers and suppliers will get the worst end of the deal of the fuel surcharge increase," said Medo Pournader, senior lecturer of supply chain management at the University of Melbourne. University of Sydney professor Ben Fahimnia, who is also a specialist on the issue, said continually pushing rising logistics costs back onto suppliers is not a sustainable solution. "They have absorbed some of the costs initially and have tried to find savings elsewhere, but there is a limit to what businesses can absorb," Professor Fahimnia said. While Professor Merkert agrees, he believes the effect is unlikely to be one-for-one. "Higher fuel levies can eventually contribute to higher retail prices and hence inflation, but freight is only one element of the final shelf price, so consumers would not necessarily see a direct or proportional increase at the check-out," he said. Rising fuel prices have played a significant part in Australia's inflation rate, which recently jumped to 4 per cent in August. Transport was the second-largest contributor to the annual inflation figure as a result of higher automotive fuel prices. The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected, with headline inflation up 4 per cent in the year to August. On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 14.8 per cent in August, compared with a rise of 7.5 per cent in July. In a press conference after last week's monetary policy decision, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock warned businesses were preparing to pass on higher fuel costs if necessary. "The longer it [the war] lasts, if businesses were thinking, "Oh, look, it'll come off, I won't pass on costs," the longer it goes, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases," Ms Bullock said.

events.title: Logan mayor warns of backyard 'slums' as council slashes granny flat tax
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Logan City Council to slash granny flat infrastructure charges despite fears of backyard 'slums' Granny flats will be cheaper to build under the new infrastructure charges scheme. ( Supplied: Housing Industry Association ) Logan City Council has voted to halve its infrastructure charges on one-bedroom granny flats. Several councillors fear the change will incentivise landlords to create more backyard "slums". The new rules are expected to come into effect in November this year. Granny flats will be $13,500 cheaper to build in Logan after controversial new rules were passed by Logan City Council today. The council voted to halve its $27,000 infrastructure charge for one-bedroom secondary dwellings to incentivise new granny flats. Logan Mayor Jon Raven opposed the move, saying it would be exploited by landlords to fit more renters onto small backyard lots. He blamed laws introduced by the Queensland government in 2022 that allowed property owners to rent granny flats to non-family members. Jon Raven says granny flats should be for families, not property investors. ( ABC News: Lucy Loram ) Cr Raven said this was a "loophole" which allowed property investors to build more developments than they would otherwise be allowed to build. He said Logan's previous attempts to incentivise more secondary dwellings caused severe suburban overcrowding due to these laws. "We saw what happened with auxiliary units where you could put a two-bedroom secondary dwelling on the same site as a three-bedroom primary dwelling," Cr Raven said. "We got slums, and we can still see them in parts of the city today, because we can't remove them once they've been approved. "Savvy investors will find a way to exploit the discount as best as possible." Councillor Nathan St Ledger supported the move, saying more families wanted to move in together due to the growing unaffordability of housing. He said council's charges were "bloody expensive" and preventing more granny flats from being built. He said this would bolster the supply of affordable housing in Logan, even if much of it was run by unscrupulous property investors. "You've got rocks in your head if you think people aren't going to do it," Cr St Ledger said. "I completely understand the problem it could cause … but what about the residents who want to do the right thing?" Under Logan's current rules, infrastructure charges can be waived entirely if the granny flat is connected to the primary house and is used for family members. The changes are expected to commence in November this year. The motion passed with the support of eight councillors, with three opposing and one abstaining. The councillors who opposed were Mindy Rusell, Paul Jackson, and Cr Raven, with Teresa Lane abstaining. events.title: Coffee prices at some cafes rise by 10pc after RBA card surcharge ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coffee prices at some cafes rise 10pc after Reserve Bank imposes card surcharge ban Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Hospitality businesses have raised prices in response to the surcharge ban. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) Cafes and restaurants have begun lifting prices in response to the RBA's surcharge ban. The ban was intended to lower prices, but the price hikes appear to be an unintended consequence. Former RBA official Luci Ellis says the ban is unlikely to have a significant impact on inflation. A ban on card surcharges has resulted in some cafe owners raising the price of their coffee. About 17 per cent of cafes are now charging more for a flat white, compared with prices prior to October 1, when the Reserve Bank's ban took effect. That is according to Small Flat White, an online platform that tracks coffee prices across more than 1,500 cafes. Typically, the increase was 50 cents, or almost 10 per cent of the coffee's price, which is much higher than the typical 0.5 to 1.5 per cent surcharge consumers used to pay on their credit or debit card transactions. Avtar Singh says most small businesses are operating on thin margins. ( ABC News ) Not every hospitality business has raised its prices in the immediate aftermath of the ban. Avtar Singh, owner of a Thai restaurant in Hobart, said he was currently absorbing the cost of the surcharges but eventually would have to raise prices. "The government needs to understand small businesses are already at a very thin margin," he told the ABC. "If you squeeze it any further, it'll come to a point where doing business is very, very difficult." Wes Lambert says the card surcharge ban has led to unintended results. ( ABC News ) Most cafes or restaurants have raised prices in some way, either by raising menu prices or increasing weekend or public holiday surcharges, said Wes Lambert, chief executive of the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association. "Increasing prices can always affect demand, so that certainly is an unintended consequence that the RBA could not have predicted, because they believed that prices would only go up 0.1 per cent," he said. Mr Lambert said some businesses had started taking cash-only payments or accepting bank transfers. "They should have known better that inflation was going to remain pesky and that this ban would come online during a cost of living crisis and potentially should have delayed the ban during this high inflationary and high interest environment." The RBA has said the previous system was no longer working as intended, with surcharges increasingly difficult for consumers to avoid. The central bank has also said only about 16 per cent of businesses were surcharging and the ban was designed to reduce card acceptance costs, particularly for small businesses. Reforms unlikely to affect interest rates Luci Ellis says the changes will not have a significant impact on inflation. ( ABC News ) If the surcharge ban results in higher inflation, that effect would likely be temporary and have no effect on interest rates, according to Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis. "Previously surcharges were imposed to reflect the cost of accepting certain types of payment; that's now been bundled into the price, so some business have increased their prices, but that's a one-off, not inherently inflationary," she said. "Most of the reports we've seen of prices increasing … more than what the surcharge had been were in hospitality. "There are plenty of other inflationary forces going round, including the pass-through of high energy costs onto other prices that the Reserve Bank's going to be much more focused on." Surcharge bans are supposed to save consumers money but retailers say they're being forced to put prices up and are finding ways around the reforms. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver agreed. "The overall macroeconomic impact from higher prices flowing from the ban on surcharges may not be that significant," he said. Mr Oliver said many large businesses were already not charging surcharges. "It's really just an issue for small businesses, but there still may be some upwards boost to inflation, albeit minor," he said. "In theory, the RBA may just look through it as it's a one-off impact, but it may be hard to disentangle a general rise in prices from the impact of the surcharge versus other factors." The Reserve Bank declined to comment.

events.title: Capital Group secures ADGM licence to expand Middle East operations
events.summary: Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, has secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager and expand operations across the region. The development comes after the company announced plans to set up its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi in May, with Capital Group relocating associates from North America, Europe and Asia to support clients in the region. The company will now be able to conduct trading, investment management and distribution activities within Abu Dhabi's financial centre, it said in a statement on Wednesday. “Establishing a regulated presence in Abu Dhabi brings us closer to our clients and to the investment opportunities across the Middle East, a region where we have been active for many years,” said Benno Klingenberg-Timm, head of Abu Dhabi office and head of institutional for Europe and Asia at Capital Group. “From day one, we will have a meaningful presence, with on-the-ground investment, operational and client-facing capabilities,” he added. The move reflects “our confidence in the region’s long-term growth”, Mr Klingenberg-Timm said. Capital Group’s expansion adds to the growing number of global investment firms setting up in Abu Dhabi. ADGM , the largest international financial centre in the Middle East and Africa by number of active licences, has continued to attract global institutions, despite the Iran war. New Mountain Capital, an alternative investment firm based in New York, said on Tuesday it was opening an office in ADGM to strengthen its presence in the Middle East. Founded in 1999, New Mountain has about $60 billion in assets under management across its private equity, credit and net lease investment strategies. “We have been privileged to work with many leading investors in the region for years and establishing a local presence will allow us to deepen those relationships while building new partnerships over time,” said Adam Weinstein, president and chief operating officer. Last week, Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, opened an office in ADGM . Global private markets firm Pantheon last week opened its first Abu Dhabi office in ADGM to expand its presence in the Middle East and tap growing demand from investors across the Gulf. A base in Abu Dhabi provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's biggest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. Other high-profile companies that the UAE capital has attracted in recent months include private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. Collectively, asset managers that established operations in ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management. Capital Group’s “decision reflects the strength of Abu Dhabi’s financial ecosystem and ADGM’s growing position as a leading international financial centre for global institutions seeking long-term opportunities across the region”, said Ahmed Al Zaabi, chairman of ADGM.

events.title: Grocery runs on a budget and outdoor missions: How S’pore banks make financial literacy fun for kids
events.summary: UOB Heartbeat volunteers Derrick Sin (left) and Jane Lai (right) with Aaron Kishen Arun Pandian Pillai, 11, and Najwa Chua Ai Xin, 12. Singapore banks teach financial literacy to primary school children through hands-on programmes like shopping trips and interactive play spaces. UOB and OCBC participate in grocery shopping trips, helping children from lower-income families make budgeting and spending decisions. DBS offers educational play areas like POSB Forestlands, combining stories and activities to make money management fun, while involving parents in the learning journey. SINGAPORE – Every two to three months, Aaron Kishen Arun Pandian Pillai, 11, and his brother Leon Shrishen, nine, join UOB volunteers on shopping trips organised by Children’s Wishing Well. Each child gets a $50 FairPrice voucher, sponsored by the bank, to purchase groceries and household essentials under the Fresh Groceries for Every Student’s Home (FRESH) programme. Children’s Wishing Well started FRESH in 2019 to teach financial literacy to children and youth from low-income families. The charity also equips these children and youth with other essential life skills, such as career readiness and personal development, through its other enrichment programmes. To stretch their dollars, the children must compare prices, prioritise needs and make their own purchasing decisions. The initiative gives the children a chance to learn more about budgeting and apply what they have learnt in school about managing their expenses. It is one of a slate of hands-on programmes supported by local banks to reinforce the lessons on saving, spending and budgeting that children are taught in primary school. UOB has partnered Children’s Wishing Well on this initiative since 2022. The July 22 shopping trip that The Straits Times tagged along on was 11-year-old Aaron’s eighth outing with volunteers from UOB Heartbeat, the bank’s flagship volunteering programme. (Clockwise from left) Aaron Kishen Arun Pandian Pillai, UOB Heartbeat volunteers Lim Gene Harn and Derrick Sin and Aaron's brother Leon Shrishen Arun Pandian Pillai discussing how to de-conflict their shopping lists. Proclaiming himself the family’s “household planner”, he remarked: “My brother will buy the wrong brand, so I have to keep an eye on him.” Aaron managed his budget tightly that day, spending $50.02, including $3.91 on sweets – just under the $4 allowed for snacks. “My school organises workshops for us to learn,” Aaron shared. “I picked up budgeting and spending tips at the workshops, which I now apply to my shopping trips.” Besides the two brothers, there were eight other child beneficiaries, each paired with a UOB volunteer. Among them was Derrick Sin, vice-president of group retail (risk), who was a volunteer on the trip for the first time. Sin, who was paired with Leon, recounted how the young boy initially wanted to buy a bunch of grapes that cost nearly $10. Knowing it would use up a fifth of his total funds, he hesitated. But after further thought, Leon chose the healthy fruit option over an unhealthy Coca-Cola drink and gave up a few other items as well. “He was able to make that trade-off himself,” said Sin, who also observed how Aaron managed his own shopping expenses. When the older boy’s assigned volunteer forgot to track the price of each item in their basket, the 11-year-old stepped up and went to the counter to verify the tally. Watching Aaron take charge, Sin was impressed. He recalled thinking, “This boy really knows what he is doing.” Jane Lai, UOB senior vice-president of talent and development, noted that the children are forced to make choices during these shopping trips and consider what they must give up if they choose one item over another. The July event was her third time volunteering, and she was paired with eight-year-old Jariss . At one point, the girl felt torn between a Korean brand of instant noodles that cost more than $8, which her sister likes, and the cheaper Indomie alternative her family had asked her to purchase. She picked the more affordable option, leaving her enough cash for a $2 snack. UOB Heartbeat volunteer Jane Lai (left) pointing out the bleach on Jariss’ shopping list. Exposing children to real-life situations builds early financial awareness to ensure that they become savvy consumers, Lai said. She mused that she should have given her two children, now in their twenties, similar hands-on shopping experiences when they were younger. “In hindsight, I would have pushed a lot more of this (financial) discipline,” she reflected. “Protected kids like ours tend to be less resilient as they grow up.” To date, UOB Heartbeat volunteers have participated in about 50 grocery shopping sessions, which are organised twice a month, supporting more than 700 children.

events.title: Abu Dhabi to upgrade Tamm app as it pursues AI-native government goal
events.summary: Abu Dhabi plans to launch the latest version of the Tamm app in December as it pursues its goal of becoming the world’s first fully AI-native government, a senior executive has said. The refreshed Tamm 5.0 app, which would be introduced at the Gitex Global technology exhibition in Dubai, promises "increasingly intelligent" services, Department of Government Enablement director general Ruba Al Hassan told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Those services are to also be more "proactive and personalised", but they still have to remain "simple and trusted", said Ms Al Hassan, who oversees strategic affairs and future foresight at the department. Tamm currently has about 4.7 million users, having grown by more than 1.5 million in just a year. About 90 per cent of its transactions are finalised within a day, the latest data from the DGE shows. Tamm 5.0 would be "another step" in the evolution from a digital government to an AI-native government, "moving towards a model where government increasingly understands context ... anticipates needs and helps people achieve things more easily", Ms Al Hassan said. The DGE did not reveal the specific changes to Tamm or new services that are to be introduced. "It’s time for the next phase, which is about making the experience even more seamless and reducing the effort required from residents, businesses and visitors," she added. The DGE remains "focused" on its goal of transforming the capital's government services into a fully AI-native platform by next year, Ms Al Hassan said. The agency is "moving with urgency, but building responsibly", she added. "We are already seeing that tangible progress across government, not only through individual AI applications, but through the foundations that make AI-native government possible," she said, referring to data, infrastructure, digital services, workforce capability and governance. "The question is not whether we can deploy AI faster, it’s whether we can create lasting value at scale, so we believe we are on the right path to do that." Abu Dhabi is boosting tech use across the emirate under its digital strategy, which focuses on five key enablers – one of them being the use of AI across public services. Despite the persisting challenges – especially issues involving AI models going rogue and compromising other websites – the DGE is seeking to ensure the safety and reliability of such systems. "We’re seeing a lot of noise in the global AI conversation. New models are constantly coming out, capabilities are getting better quickly and everyone’s focused on what might happen in the future," Ms Al Hassan said. "Our focus is slightly different. We’re interested in where AI delivers practical value today ... we also believe trust is critical. People need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with clear human accountability." Educating users is also a key part of the DGE's mandate, she said. "As AI improves, the value of human judgment actually also increases. People need to know how to work effectively with AI, challenge AI outputs and make better decisions," she said. "When it comes to AI, the skill won’t be coding, it will be maintaining judgment." 'Most powerful generation' Meanwhile, Omar Al Olama, Minister of State for AI, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, described the present generation as the "most powerful in human history", while calling for more responsible use of AI. "The reason ... is because you have the intelligence of every single generation, every single human that has lived, that has actually produced something that has lasted ... the content and knowledge are at your fingertips," he told the conference. "And you don't just have raw knowledge. You're actually able to leverage intelligence to do something with it through agentic AI," he added, referring to the class designed to make autonomous decisions and act with minimal human supervision. "This is the time for a new ambitious generation ... people might not believe in your ideas, to wield these tools to create something that others can't see or don't believe is possible. It's a calling."

events.title: Microsoft defines its Azure instance lifecycle, without any info about timing
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Redmond explains how VMs die, but not when you can expect that to happen Dutch tax office ditches Microsoft 365 cloud for on-premises alternative 3 hours ago Microsoft extends the Outlook naughty step with two more file types 1 day ago Classic Outlook clings to stale search results as Microsoft works on a fix 1 day ago Windows 11 market share creeps upwards as cost of staying on Windows 10 set to double 2 days ago Flight delayed? So are these codec updates 5 days ago Microsoft has updated the lifecycle of an Azure instance, without offering any information on how long it takes for an instance type to expire. Redmond’s “enhanced lifecycle” landed in late September in a post that explains the four phases in the life of a cloudy VM: Current – VMs are recommended for new deployments, are available in many regions, and receive standard maintenance and support; Extended – Still supported, but may be subject to usage quotas and unspecified “changes to purchasing options and pricing.” Microsoft recommends planning a move to Current VMs. End of Life – VMs are still supported but are only available to existing customers and you may not be able to get more of the instances you want. Once VMs reach this stage, Microsoft wants you “actively” working to shift workloads onto Current or Extended VMs. Retired – Unsupported but not quite dead. Microsoft says VMs in this phase are no longer available and have been “deallocated” – Azure-speak for not having an IP address and being dormant, with data preserved. Customers can’t provision the instance types. Microsoft’s post explains that the company defined this lifecycle because it is “committed to helping you navigate these infrastructure transitions and take advantage of the next wave of innovation.” The post includes many mentions of “modernization” – the process of moving to Current Azure instance types. “As Azure continues to advance, our commitment is to make change predictable, transparent, and supported through clear lifecycle guidance, early visibility, and practical help to modernize with confidence,” the post states. The mention of “predictable” change led The Register to wonder if the lifecycle has a predictable cadence that means users can expect that instance types will remain in “Current” status for a certain number of years. We asked Microsoft if its Azure instance lifecycles are timed, and a spokesperson sent the following comment: “As Azure continues to innovate, we regularly evolve our infrastructure to give customers access to newer technologies and capabilities. As part of our updated Azure Virtual Machines lifecycle, we will continue to provide customers with advance notice when select older-generation VM series enter the End of Life stage. We’re giving customers time, guidance and resources to plan their transition to the current VM generations, while continuing to support Azure VMs through their lifecycle in alignment with the policies we published.” The spokesperson added that Microsoft customers are “notified directly about their specific VM retirements.” For what it’s worth, Microsoft publishes retirement announcements for Azure services . The company has also previously revealed it runs Azure servers for six years. It is unclear if the new Azure lifecycle is tied to that hardware retirement schedule. What is clear is that Microsoft wants Azure customers to regularly consider moving to its latest instance types. That’s a reasonable suggestion given that newer VMs will likely use more powerful processors. There’s also plenty of upside for Microsoft because more recent silicon typically offers more cores per die, and better performance-per-watt. Microsoft therefore gets greater processor density with lower energy consumption, which lowers its operating costs. Let’s see if Redmond’s lifecycle tweaks also see it pass on those savings.

events.title: News anchor Richard Morecroft remembered as a 'great Australian'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft remembered for wit and generosity Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft is being remembered as a consummate professional and "a great Australian". The 70-year-old died "at a time of his choosing", a statement on Instagram said, after he received a cancer diagnosis earlier this year. "We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," the statement said. Morecroft graced television screens for decades as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor for almost 20 years, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS. Doogue (left) and Morecroft presenting the news together. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Geraldine Doogue worked with Morecroft as co-host on The National in 1985, when her late husband Ian Carroll changed the half-hour 7PM television bulletin to an hour-long news and current affairs program. Doogue told 702 ABC Sydney that she was shocked by his death and said his professionalism was a big part of his legacy. "He was just terribly good to me and to my late husband ... during that really tumultuous year," she said. "I mean, he was very much for it. Richard, once he was in, he was in. He was a very loyal, he contributed massively." Veteran news anchor and television presenter, Richard Morecroft, is being remembered in tributes. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Doogue said he had a strong sense of what "an ABC authority ought to be" and modelled it "effortlessly". "He had quite a wit about him, but he fundamentally felt his role, I think, was to be that face of the ABC while he was doing this," she said. He also hosted wildlife and educational programs and wrote about nature and the environment. Morecroft eventually moved to the NSW south coast, which Doogue said he called "his cathedral", with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay. "He had this whole side in him that was artistic, very much involved with the natural world," she said. "He just thrived in that environment and gave enormously to [and was] very generous to all sorts of charities." Australian Story ABC presenter and friend, Leigh Sales, told ABC 702 Sydney Mornings she first saw Morecroft on TV while watching Behind the News at school in the 1980s. Sales says Morecroft spoke with her just after she started working at the ABC. Sales said when she moved from Brisbane to Sydney as a young reporter at 22, he checked in with her to see how she was settling in. Sales is often seen speaking with young journalists and producers, helping to foster the next generation. "I try really hard to be a good listener and to not be just telling people, 'Well, here's how I do it'," she said. "The other thing that I feel like I learned from him is it doesn't matter if you're the star, you muck in like one of the team and you're not better than anyone else." Richard Morecroft at the 2025 Sculpture in the Valley festival with festival director Stuart McCreery. ( ABC News: ABC Illawarra/Rory Macdonald ) Former ABC presenter Keith Conlon, who met Morecroft when they worked together at a student radio station in Adelaide in the 1970s, said his fellow broadcaster was always a "lovely, warm person". "We kind of invented community radio on the run, and Richard was one of those people who came through the door — he was an arts student [at University of Adelaide]," he said. "He wasn't one of those 'out there' types … Very articulate, very intelligent. Conlon said originally, Morecroft expressed interest in potentially becoming a teacher or an actor, but that it made sense he turned to news reading. "If you're a newsreader, you are in a way acting. You only run the gamut from A to B but you've got to try to lift that news off the page and give things a different nuance," he said. Conlon said Morecroft had "a twinkle in his eye". ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) Conlon said he was "delightful" with "a twinkle in his eye". "He had a beautiful voice — just that lovely tone, but much more than that, he had a considered way of talking," he said. "He loved the language, he loved the sense of what we were talking about, and he was dedicated to doing those things right. He was a perfectionist. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that Morecroft was a "great Australian". "Combining a consummate professionalism with an unyielding humanity, Richard was a figure of absolute trust, a warm and familiar presence who guided us through the good times and bad," he said. "He loved the arts and was deeply passionate about our natural environment.

events.title: Landowner pushes back against opposition to Goolwa's first McDonald's
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Regional Development and Planning If the application is successful, it will be Goolwa's first chain-based fast-food outlet. ( ABC News ) A property in Goolwa is under contract to the fast-food giant, subject to state planning approval. The landowner says a McDonald's in Goolwa will employ young people and bring increased competition for takeaway food. An application is expected to be made to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon. The landowner where Goolwa's first McDonald's could be built has pushed back against local opposition, saying residents have a "democratic right" to choose what to eat or drink. Mick McArdle's commercial property at Hutchinson Street is under contract to the fast-food giant, subject to approval of a development application expected to be lodged with the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon. But it has faced vocal opposition, first from a volunteer group dedicated to protecting Goolwa's culinary and cultural heritage, and then from Alexandrina Council, which recently voted to oppose establishing chain-based fast-food outlets in the seaside town. The property is under contract and a development application is expected soon. ( 891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn ) "I don't think that people should have the right to take away other people's democratic right to choose what they eat or drink," Mr McArdle said. "A lot of people actually like the idea of having a McDonald's here. Alexandrina Council last month voted in favour of Cr Peter Oliver's motion, which stated that 38 food outlets in the area, including restaurants, cafes, supermarkets and service stations, already offer food. The motion passed, but not unanimously. It followed lobbying by Cittaslow Goolwa, a volunteer group of about 250 members. Goolwa was the first Australian town to be accredited by Cittaslow International in 2007, a European movement that promotes quality of life and sustainability in towns and cities, and handed a "slow town" status . Cittaslow Goolwa vice-president Christine Putland said recently that the town already sold takeaway hamburgers and did not need to rely on a "multinational company" to create more . "Even if the franchises might be more local or state-based, it is still not growing out of the community," she said in August. A Cittaslow delegation travelled to Goolwa from Italy in 2007 to present the council with a certificate. ( Website: Cittaslow Goolwa ) But Mr McArdle, who has lived in the town since 1978 and runs an automotive repair business on the site, said a significant portion of the town's population of more than 8,000 wanted a McDonald's because it would give young people work, and create more competition for takeaway food. "Competition has to be good for the people in Goolwa; competition keeps the prices at a reasonable level," Mr McArdle said. "And one of the service stations where you come into town has golden fried chicken, pizzas, the whole lot. He acknowledged he had a vested interest in the situation, but pointed out members of Cittaslow Goolwa involved with food outlets did as well. "At the end of the day, if the development application ticks all the boxes as far as zoning and all that sort of stuff, then why should they [McDonald's] not be able to go in there?" Mr McArdle said. Advocates for Goolwa's heritage attractions say the site of a former automotive repair business has been targeted for a McDonald's. Alexandrina Council Mayor Keith Parkes said there were "definitely people in the town" who backed a McDonald's but "the vast majority didn't". "It would be interesting to know whether the people that are in favour are long-term residents or fairly new residents to the area," he said. He agreed that a McDonald's would require local staff. "However, the small businesses in the town at the moment and around the place, struggle to get staff as it is, particularly in the hospitality area," Mr Parkes said. Aside from a McDonald's at the top of the Fleurieu Peninsula at Aldinga, there is only one other McDonald's on the peninsula, which is located 17 kilometres to Goolwa's west at Victor Harbor. "It will be very interesting, when eventually all the information comes out in the open, just where we stand with who's for and who's against it, and their reasons," Mr Parkes said. He reiterated that any development application requiring a change of use for the site would not go to the council for consideration. It would go to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel — an independent body established under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016.

events.title: Licence granted for controversial mineral sands mine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Avonbank Mineral Sands Project near Horsham granted licence by Victorian regulator WIM Resource dug a test pit, which it then grew barley and lentil crops on. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) Resources Victoria has approved a mining licence for the Avonbank Mineral Sands Project in Dooen, near Horsham. The WIM Resource-operated mine was granted a 20-year licence to dig up materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy projects. WIM Resource says construction could start in late 2027, with the mine to be operational by 2029, pending finances, construction and environmental approvals. Victoria's mining regulator has granted a 20-year licence for a controversial mineral sands mine near Horsham in Victoria's west. Resources Victoria granted the licence to the WIM Resource Avonbank project in Dooen, 15 kilometres north-east of Horsham, licensing the company to mine heavy mineral sands including zircon, titanium and rare earth elements. The mine site will cover about 3,400 hectares, with the Chinese-backed company planning to mine around the clock for materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy infrastructure. The company said construction could begin late next year, with mining starting in 2029, pending finances and other construction and environmental approvals. "This is a major moment for Avonbank, but just as importantly, it is a major moment for the Wimmera Southern Mallee," said the WIM Resource executive team of Eddy Wu and Michael Winternitz in a statement. The company plans to operate the mine for 36 years, digging up 12.75 million tonnes of heavy mineral concentrate. It has done so in the face of stiff opposition from residents and the local council, which has previously labelled the company's attitude to community concerns "disgusting". "Going by my phone calls … I think there's some people absolutely devastated in the community," said Horsham Rural City Council Mayor Brian Klowss. Brian Klowss says the community remains unhappy with the mining company's plans. ( Supplied: Rural Press Club of Victoria ) The Victorian government's mining regulator said it approved the company's licence after determining it had an "appropriate program of work", which it could finance and complete. However, it rejected the company's request for a 38-year-licence. The Horsham Rural City Council has previously raised numerous concerns about the proposed mine, including dust issues, and concerns with use of the nearby intermodal freight hub and rehabilitation prospects of the land. Resources Victoria said mineral handling procedures, real-time onsite monitoring and the mine's operating hours would be finalised as part of the work plan assessment. The mine site is near Dooen, a rural village in the Wimmera region. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) "This outcome is as a result of diligent assessment work by numerous agencies and departments at both the state and Commonwealth level," said Resources Victoria director for regulatory operations, Laura Helm. But Cr Klowss said many in the community felt their voices had not been heard, and that he was "dubious" about the site's rehabilitation plans. He said while some concerns had been considered, questions remained about real-time air monitoring and a potential mining licence for the nearby freight hub. "They're devastated about what it's going to do to our community," he said. Cr Klowss said he was told to expect a licensing decision in January, and that former planning minister Lily D'Ambrosio and current minister Sonya Kilkenny would not speak to council about the mine. "I'm actually probably curious to know why the decision was made now," he said. The ABC has contacted the Victorian government for a response. Victorian Farmers Federation (VFF) president Ryan Milgate said the licensing approval on the eve of an election was fundamentally at odds with the VFF's call for a pause on new critical minerals projects. The mine site will cover about 3,400 hectares. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Avonbank mine is one of 10 mineral sands projects planned for the Wimmera-Mallee and across the New South Wales border. WIM Resource said it estimated the project, when complete, would support 1,000 full-time local jobs, and that it would continue to work with traditional owners, councils, landowners, businesses and the broader community. The company also said it would provide a $40 million community benefit fund, progressively funded over the life of the mine, that would provide long-term investment for communities across the region. WIM Resource says the mine will support the community.

events.title: Musk’s SpaceX in talks to borrow US$40 billion to buy Nvidia chips
events.summary: SpaceX is seeking to raise about US$10 billion (S$12.8 billion) in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips. SpaceX is seeking US$40 billion, led by Apollo Global Management, to buy Nvidia chips, showing huge demand for AI computing power. The plan includes US$10 billion in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt, with the deal expected to close in 2027. The report highlights rising costs and heavy AI spending, while SpaceX shares fell and Nvidia’s stock rose after the news. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise US$40 billion (S$51.1 billion) of debt to buy chips from Nvidia, sources familiar with the matter said, underscoring the insatiable demand among AI developers for more computing power. Pacific Investment Management is one of the investment managers looking at the deal, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the talks are private. SpaceX’s fund-raising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said. Musk’s AI, satellite and rocket conglomerate is seeking to raise about US$10 billion in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips, the Financial Times reported earlier, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. Apollo Global Management is leading the financing, in a deal that is expected to close in 2027, the newspaper said. Tech companies and artificial intelligence model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips to power AI systems. The worldwide expansion of computing capacity has sent the costs of everything from land to chips and power-generation equipment soaring, touching off a series of massive financing deals. Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Times’ report. SpaceX shares erased gains in postmarket trading following the FT’s report, falling 1.2% in US postmarket trading to $169.79. Nvidia’s stock rose fractionally. In September , Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by the end of 2026 . It was the most detailed timetable that the trillionaire has given yet for expansion plans for the Memphis-area cluster. Colossus 2 now has 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s, Musk said in a post on X. A further 220,000 GB300s are due to be operational next week, with another 220,000 expected in November, he said. An additional 220,000 may come online late December “if we get lucky”, he said. Musk’s xAI has recruited multiple Wall Street firms to test its Grok chatbot, including Apollo and Morgan Stanley. Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source US$500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure. The coalition – which also includes Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group and KKR & Co. – said at the time that they would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers”. Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signalled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify towards this commitment. events.title: Why Darwin could become 'a major interconnection point' for global data
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Darwin could host multiple international subsea cables amid NT government's digital infrastructure push Topic: Urban Development and Planning The developments have been pitched for the Darwin suburb of Fannie Bay. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Development applications show Google and Inligo Networks want to connect subsea fibre-optic cables to infrastructure in Darwin's Fannie Bay. Telecom analysts and the government say the NT capital city is optimally placed to serve markets in south-east Asia and Australia's southern states. Darwin is becoming a "network ecosystem" of subsea cables, terrestrial cables and data centres, Mr Tan says, which has been embraced by the NT government. As data centres and fibre-optic cable networks proliferate globally, planning documents show two international subsea cables could soon dock in the Darwin suburb of Fannie Bay. An application lodged with the Development Consent Authority shows tech giant Google plans to connect its "Bosun" subsea cable to infrastructure on the corner of Atkin Drive and Conacher Street. Subsea cables are fibre-optic wires which run along the ocean floor, transmitting data to onshore landing stations and facilitating intercontinental internet traffic. The planning application does not detail what the telecom infrastructure at the site will be. The proposed development is located near the Darwin Ski Club, at the corner of Atkin Drive and Conacher Street. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) If approved, Bosun will travel through telecommunication conduits — connected to the Fannie Bay site — to Christmas Island , where there is onward connectivity to Singapore. Bosun forms part of Google's Connect Australia initiative , a network of fibre-optic cables connecting Darwin and Perth to the east coast and trans-Pacific cable networks. On the parcel of land directly opposite the proposed Bosun site, multinational subsea cable company Inligo Networks is building Darwin's first "open" cable landing station. According to designs published by Inligo, the station will comprise a single-storey building and is set to harbour part of Inligo's Asia Connect Cable System (ACC-1). Designs for the building planned by Inligo Digital Australia's open cable landing station at Fannie Bay. ( Supplied: Inligo ) Once complete, ACC-1 will connect Darwin to four Indonesian cities, East-Timor, Singapore, the Philippines, Guam and the US mainland. It will also connect to Inligo's Unite Cable System — a network linking Darwin, Adelaide and Melbourne, granted major project status under the former NT government. The facility's "open" status means it will be accessible to multiple telecommunication companies and service providers looking to use one of the cables for their networks. Darwin is on track to host five international subsea cables in the coming years, with major tech firms seeking to exploit the city's proximity to south-east Asia and the Pacific. The NT's first international subsea cable, Vocus's Darwin-Jakarta-Singapore Cable system (DJSC), went online in July 2023 following a government investment of nearly $8 million. The lot is typically used by Darwin Ski Club patrons for overflow parking. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Hawaiki Nui 1, a subsea cable stretching from Singapore to Sydney via the Indo-Pacific, is being developed by digital infrastructure company BW Digital. Meanwhile, Meta's gargantuan Project Waterworth is on track to stretch around the world — from the United States' east to west coast — will also connect to Australia via Darwin. Marvin Tan, a senior research analyst from telecom research group TeleGeography, said Darwin is optimally placed to serve markets in south-east Asia and Australia's southern states. Marvin Tan says Darwin's geographic proximity to south-east Asia means it can service international markets wanting to bypass the South China Sea. ( Supplied ) "Traditionally, cables reached the eastern parts or the western parts of Australia, but now you can simply tap into Darwin and the terrestrial network to reach both," he said. Mr Tan also noted Australia's geopolitical stability and robust legal system, which he said make it an optimal location for data centres and, subsequently, subsea cable development. Google plans to connect its Bosun subsea cable to infrastructure in Fannie Bay. ( Supplied: FYFE/Google Earth ) Darwin specifically gives international proponents of data centres and subsea cables an opportunity to bypass the South China Sea. "Instead of going from Singapore to Japan and the United States, you can go south to Darwin and then back to the US, like with Project Waterworth and ACC-1," Mr Tan said.

events.title: Anthropic reconfigures its cool kids security program
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Company's Project Glasswing and Cyber Verification Program metamorphose into triple tier threat hunting club Poetry is the new AI security threat as PoeLLM malware infects 3K+ servers now Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 18 hours ago Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it 2 days ago Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 2 days ago Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows 4 days ago Only a week after warning about the perils of competitor Z.ai's GLM-5.3 model and its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Anthropic has expanded its Cyber Verification Program (CVP) – or rather, reconfigured it. "For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP," the AI biz said . "Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems." Project Glasswing and CVP launched in April 2026 alongside the debut of Mythos, the company's highly capable and equally hyped frontier model. Project Glasswing gave partners early access to Mythos so they could scour their systems for vulnerabilities before attackers beat them to it. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity was not particularly impressed with CVEs identified by Project Glasswing, noting that fewer than 0.5 percent of the 225 Anthropic-linked vulnerabilities he tracked were being exploited in the wild. And Anthropic's own warning last month about the risks posed by GLM-5.3 somewhat undermines the idea that there's anything special about its own Mythos model. Even so, Anthropic says that its security program has allowed its partners to spot at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And the biz claims that its own open source scanning efforts revealed an additional 5,500 verified vulnerabilities between April and October. "Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity," Anthropic said. "This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher." When these might get patched is unclear. The company's own figures indicate that of 5,674 true positive vulnerabilities, 3,014 are high severity, and 1,522 are critical severity, yet only 516 have been patched. Given industry boasting about the cybersecurity prowess of AI models, generating a fix, testing it, and deploying it ought to be nearly automatic at this point. But the gap between identification and remediation suggests there's a lot of slack in the system that needs to be ironed out. Two programs into one with three tiers Now Anthropic's two programs, one intended for organizations and one for individual security professionals, have been merged and reconfigured into three tiers. The AI biz has not explained why, but its stated intent is to tie model capabilities to specific tasks: Defense Access, Red Team Access, and Specialized Access. Depending on the tier, participants will encounter more or fewer blocks on security-related tasks. As a measure of program participation value, Anthropic said that based on five attempts at 10 CyScenarioBench challenges, those without CVP access got blocked on every attempt. Defense Access is intended for security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government organizations that focus on system defense. In this tier, Claude Opus 5.5 faced refusals in 46 of 50 attempts and succeeded four times. Red Team Access is for penetration testing and offensive cyber evaluation, and participants will still face model refusals for model interactions that would cause physical harm or mass disruption.

events.title: Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up
events.summary: Google on Tuesday struck a deal with Constellation Energy for 3,590 megawatts of future energy supply, including nearly a gigawatt of new nuclear capacity, as the search and advertising giant tries to find enough energy to power its datacenter ambitions. The 20-year power purchase agreement will see Constellation, the largest purveyor of atomic energy in the US, bring an additional 890 megawatts of nuclear capacity online by making "targeted investments at multiple nuclear plants." We understand those investments will go toward upgrades to at least 11 existing nuclear plants across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey through a process known as uprating. "By modernizing and upgrading turbines, steam generators, and digital control systems at operating plants, uprates deliver substantial capacity gains without the multi-year timelines or interconnection bottlenecks associated with greenfield construction," the power company explained in a statement. The other 2,700 megawatts the deal covers will come from other unspecified sources. Constellation expects to spend $4.3 billion to fulfill its side of the deal, and plans to complete its first uprated reactor by 2028. Google is on track to spend as much as $205 billion on datacenters and compute this year, but all that money is wasted if it can't secure power to make its servers and GPUs work. The hyperscaler is far from the only one scrambling to secure adequate power to keep its AI ambitions from starving. Microsoft also tapped Constellation to reignite the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor – you know, the one that didn't partially melt down back in 1979. That reactor is expected to come online as early as next year. Meta is also making noise about nuclear. The Social Network is working with Constellation to save a doomed nuclear plant in Illinois. Earlier this year, Meta revealed that its nuclear and clean energy commitments now total 6.6 gigawatts, though it's worth noting that figure depends heavily on the successful rollout of small modular reactors, an unproven form of miniature nuke plant. ®

events.title: ATO will not budge on credit card ban after meeting with business groups
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ATO will not budge after snap meeting over credit card ban New regulation has put a ban on card surcharges. ( Adobe Stock ) Business groups have accused the ATO of having "double standards" for refusing to accept credit card payments from November 30. The tax office said it was not appropriate for it to absorb the surcharge fees itself because that would effectively transfer the cost to the taxpayer. The ATO has stood firm on its decision, despite calling a special forum for frustrated small business groups to discuss the changes. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) will not budge on its decision to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1, after holding a snap crisis meeting with business groups angered by the move. Australia's tax chief convened a meeting with business groups this morning to the discuss the changes in the wake of widespread backlash. But the ATO has indicated it is not going to reverse the credit card ban, according to a spokesperson from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), which attended the meeting. "We will continue to seek to have the ban overturned," the ACCI spokesperson said. The ABC has approached the ATO for comment. Last week the tax office announced it would stop accepting credit card payments at the end of next month. That step came in response to the Reserve Bank of Australia's reforms to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank said was "in the public interest" and would save customers about $1.6 billion a year. The ATO said it would continue accepting credit cards until November 30 to allow for a transition period, saying it was untenable beyond that point. Small business owners say they have been expected to absorb the fees of card transactions themselves, and have lost the option of using credit card payments to the ATO as a cash flow method. Some feared the sudden change would mean they needed to source cash quickly to begin paying by debit instead, or they would be forced to go into arrears with the ATO, and that could result in enforcement against their businesses, including possible closure. Earlier Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), had called for the ATO's credit card ban to be reversed. "There is a clear double standard here. Government is telling small business to absorb the hit from the surcharge ban and its cost, while the tax office is saying a different set of rules applies to it," he said. "Small business is the backbone of the economy. They are doing it tough, with rising costs and a fourth interest rate increase last week." There are some big changes coming for credit and debit card holders, but not all of it is good news. Here's what you need to know and how it could affect you. The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA) said it raised issues for businesses that used credit cards as a cash flow tool and said the decision "warrants a rethink". "However, the broader issue remains the card surcharge ban itself," it said in a statement, adding it was concerned about the capacity of small businesses to take on the cost. "The ATO's own response highlights that concern," it said. Master Builders CEO Denita Wawn said the surcharge card ban and other regulatory decisions were made "without consultation" and showed a "lack of practical understanding of the impact of decisions being made by this government". "It's quite incredulous," she told News 24 yesterday afternoon. The ABC understands business groups were frustrated by the meeting, and it was unclear who had made the decision to end credit card payments, and when. ATO says absorbing costs 'not tenable' In a statement on October 2, taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but credit card companies declined to offer a rate that was low enough. "The costs associated with accepting credit card payments are significant, with merchant fees estimated to be almost $200 million annually and expected to continue increasing over time," he said in the statement. "It is not tenable for the ATO to absorb the costs associated with accepting credit cards on an ongoing basis. Small business have criticised the ATO over its credit card ban. ( ABC News: Nassim Khadem ) Opposition Leader Angus Taylor called for the government to "instruct" the ATO to reverse its decision.

events.title: "You suck": Emmer unloads on Senate Republicans
events.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is saying out loud what House Republicans have been grumbling about for much of the year: They're fed up with the Senate. Why it matters You won't ever hear Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) or Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) talk about their Senate counterparts like this. "There are no Democrats. There are no Republicans. They are just senators," Emmer told donors last week at a closed-door fundraiser Axios attended for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.). Emmer said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) "is doing the job that he thinks he's supposed to do. There's a certain fraternity sorority that is the U.S. Senate." The intrigue: Emmer had a blunt message for senators who repeatedly say they can't pass House GOP priorities: "Don't just keep telling me 'Don't have the votes. Don't have the votes.' You suck." Emmer said he once thought as a House member that he should stay out of the filibuster debate. Now, he thinks his colleagues should "get rid of the darn filibuster." A Senate GOP aide retorted that what would "suck" would be losing the majority and that Republicans should be targeting Democrats instead of attacking their own side. Driving the news: Emmer's comments are the most critical yet from a House GOP leader, but sum up the mood inside the conference. More than a dozen Republicans paralyzed the House floor this summer in an effort to force Senate action on the SAVE America Act, the GOP's signature election bill that's become a major source of tension between the two chambers. "We're frustrated with the Senate," Emmer told Axios in an interview after the fundraiser. "We feel like we've been doing everything we were hired to do, and a lot of it goes over to the Senate and it just sits there." House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes. The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But there's a clear implication in that phrase: The Senate hasn't. Johnson has pointed to the backlog across the Capitol — including when he defended sending the House home early last month by noting that hundreds of House-passed bills were awaiting Senate action. The speaker blames Democrats for that, but his complaints have put the spotlight on Senate GOP leadership. Zoom in: Congressional Republicans spent much of the summer on completely different wavelengths over reconciliation 3.0 , which doesn't require any Democratic votes. Johnson pushed the Senate to take up the House's reconciliation framework, declaring in July that the Senate would pass it before leaving for August recess. "That'd be news to me," Thune said at the time about Johnson's floated timeline. The Senate left town without any action on reconciliation 3.0. "They can say all day long, you know, 'It's going to be hard.' Everything's hard. Give me a lecture about how hard things are. That's what I do every day. They've got to figure out a way to get it done," Scalise told Axios of his colleagues in the Senate in July. The bottom line: Emmer stopped short of saying Senate Republicans have been a bigger obstacle to the GOP agenda than Democrats. But he said two things frustrate lawmakers in the House when it comes to Senate Republicans: 1) They don't say what changes would get them to yes; and 2) they don't put themselves on the record when the answer is no. "Put your money where your mouth is. Put your vote up on the board, and let's see where you really are," Emmer told Axios.
