events.title: House GOP leaders admit redistricting fell short
events.summary: House GOP leaders are now openly acknowledging that their mid-decade redistricting push didn't work out as well as they'd hoped. Why it matters: Republicans kicked off the redistricting wars hoping new maps would give them a bigger cushion against the historical headwinds facing the president's party. That advantage is looking a lot smaller than they envisioned. Driving the news: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios that Republicans won't win all 13 seats they'd hoped to gain from new maps. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," Emmer told Axios aboard a plane Thursday between campaign stops in North Carolina and Virginia. Emmer echoed House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), who told Axios last month that Republicans were unlikely to sweep all 13. Zoom in: Emmer said he'd be "surprised" if Republicans sweep all five newly drawn seats in Texas and "shocked" if they win all four in Florida . But he said Republicans are certain to pick up newly drawn seats in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee. At a fundraiser for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) on Thursday, Emmer told donors that Republicans could also offset losses with pickups in Maine and potentially North Carolina, Ohio, New Mexico and Washington. Even assuming Republicans lose five seats because of redistricting in California and Utah, pickups elsewhere give the party a path to come out ahead, Emmer told donors. State of play: Redistricting still gave Republicans an edge, just smaller than they once thought. The Cook Political Report now projects Republicans will net around four seats from redistricting alone, down from the double-digit gains Republicans once hoped to squeeze from new maps. Democrats' maps in California and Utah — in response to a new Texas map — offset the GOP gains. Some newly drawn Republican pickup opportunities have become more competitive than expected. The bottom line: Democrats need to net just three seats to win the House, and the broader battlefield is moving in their direction. Cook shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later. Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

The supplies from South Korea made up 31 per cent of Russian fuel imports in August. Relations between South Korea and Ukraine are strained. Russia has imported fuel from South Korean ports, easing the impact of a fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukraine's top sanctions official says. More than 176,000 tonnes of petroleum products from South Korean ports in July and August were imported by Russia, Ukraine's top sanctions official Vladyslav Vlasiuk said on Tuesday. The supplies from South Korea made up 31 per cent of Russian fuel imports in August, according to Mr Vlasiuk, citing what he said were reports that tankers, including ones under Western sanctions, were used for the deliveries. "These shipments began precisely when Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were reducing processing volumes and creating a fuel shortage within Russia," Mr Vlasiuk, presidential commissioner for Ukrainian sanctions policy, wrote on Facebook. His comments come amid a diplomatic row between Seoul and Kyiv that erupted last month when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, a step that Seoul says was meant to stay secret. Ukraine has used long-range drones to attack Russian oil refineries and depots this year in what Kyiv has described as an effort to impose greater costs on its enemy, with no end in sight more than four years since Russia's full-scale invasion. Seoul says it continues to support efforts to end war in Ukraine. ( Reuters: Kim Soo-hyeon ) The strikes prompted Russia to impose a ban on diesel and gasoline exports, while restricting fuel purchases in some regions hit hard by the fuel crunch. "In effect, imports from South Korea helped Russia offset the impact of losing its own refining capacity," Mr Vlasiuk said, citing "available data" and "reports" as sources in his post. Earlier on Tuesday, the Guardian news agency reported that it had analysed port records and ship-tracking data, determining that the volumes were loaded at South Korean ports onto seven tankers, some of which are under UK and EU sanctions. Mr Vlasiuk provided the same figures as those in the Guardian. In response to the Guardian article, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said "the Korean government supports and actively participates in global efforts to end the war in Ukraine and achieve peaceful recovery". It said that its government was strictly enforcing export controls against Russia by expanding the scope beyond strategic items to include "non-strategic items … that carry a high risk of diversion for military use." Relations between South Korea and Ukraine have been under strain for weeks. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung threatened unspecified measures against Ukraine on Friday unless Kyiv acknowledged a confidentiality agreement that Seoul says covered the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers. Seoul has said it wants an apology. Ukraine denies there was a confidentiality agreement, but its foreign minister has said that Kyiv wants to mend ties with South Korea.

events.title: Watchdog identifies 'psychological harm' at world's largest lithium mine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Talison Lithium on notice after WorkSafe finds psychological distress among Greenbushes workers The Greenbushes mine has been described as a toxic workplace. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) WorkSafe has found poor workplace culture and conditions at Talison's Greenbushes Lithium Mine have left workers exposed to significant psychological harm. Staff say excessive demands, poor resourcing and work areas contaminated with animal faeces contributed to a toxic workplace culture. Talison says it is fast-tracking changes to workplace culture and safety. The owner of the world's largest lithium mine has been put on notice after a probe by Western Australia's work safety watchdog found a toxic workplace culture and psychologically distressed workforce. WorkSafe issued an improvement notice to Talison Lithium in August after survey responses indicated workers were exposed to psychosocial hazards at its Greenbushes mine, 240 kilometres south of Perth. Talison Lithium employs more than 1,500 workers at its Greenbushes site. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) The survey identified excessive work demands, inadequate resourcing and poor work conditions as factors in an environment causing significant psychosocial harm to staff. Reported issues included inadequate toilet facilities and working areas contaminated by animal faeces. Current and former staff who have spoken to the ABC described a toxic workplace culture. One worker, speaking anonymously due to the risk to their ongoing employment, said they felt morally distressed by what they witnessed at work and raised concerns over the independence of Talison's internal complaints process. "Employees go externally when they feel they've exhausted everything internally," they said. Workers also reported tiredness, nervousness or anxiety, low mood or depression, hopelessness and feelings of worthlessness. Greenbushes provides about 20 per cent of the world's lithium, which is considered crucial for the global energy transition. In an email sent to staff and seen by the ABC, Talison chief executive Rob Telford apologised to workers whose experience had fallen short of expectations of a respectful and safe workplace. "Let me be clear, any behaviour that undermines this, including bullying, aggression, intimidation, and any form of harassment, sexual or otherwise, has absolutely no place at Talison," Mr Telford wrote. Rob Telford says the findings of a psychosocial survey are deeply concerning. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) WorkSafe ordered Talison to complete the review of measures to manage psychosocial hazards at Greenbushes mine and consult with workers by November 20. It has ordered the review to consider interaction between job demands, worker control, role clarity, organisational change, consultation, leadership behaviours, reporting arrangements and workplace conditions. A Talison spokesperson said work had begun on improving the workplace culture before the improvement notice was issued. "Improvements have been implemented across a number of areas including clearer expectations for respectful workplace behaviour, increased team capacity, stronger systems and a sitewide program to improve facilities," they said in a statement. "Further work is planned, leveraging work that others in the industry have successfully trialled, but we have prioritised initiatives to support improving the felt experience of our workforce." The spokesperson acknowledged the findings of the psychosocial safety survey and improvement notice, and said the safety of its workforce was its priority. "[We are] working closely with our workforce and the regulator to address the matters which have been raised," the spokesperson said. The demand for lithium is being driven by batteries and electric cars. ( ABC South West: Ruslan Kulski ) "Any improvements we can make on the advice of the regulator to ensure our people continue to be treated with respect, feel safe at work, and can perform at their best, remains a focus for us. "This includes working with the regulator to fast-track changes and expedite a safety plan that was already in the process of being implemented." The spokesperson said employees were encouraged to raise concerns through a range of channels and that concerns were taken seriously. Australian Manufacturing Workers Union state secretary Steve McCartney said WorkSafe needed to take stronger action. "The feedback I'm getting is that it sounds pretty toxic, and the company is doing little or nothing to deal with it, except the review that has been there for quite some time," he said.

events.title: CDC: Monitoring Russian plague risk, "prepared" for any threat
events.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia and says it is prepared for any threat that emerges. Why it matters: Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous form of plague and is almost always fatal unless if left untreated. The latest: President Trump told reporters Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to discuss the suspected plague case and would speak with him "very soon." Asked what U.S. intelligence was saying about the situation, Trump said officials were in "very deep discussions" and that "we'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow." Catch up quick: Darya Shipilova , a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, died after reports that she may have been exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Russian authorities say testing has not linked her death to plague or to pathogens she handled at work. However, at least five hospitals in the area remain in quarantine and almost 200 people who had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation as a precaution. What they're saying: "We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available," the CDC said in an X post Tuesday. "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely." Context: The CDC said the plague is a dangerous bacterial disease that can be treated with antibiotics, especially when caught early. Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. The CDC says "rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals" are important for keeping people safe. State of play: The concerns have drawn attention on social media and from government officials and the White House. President Trump acknowledged Monday that he is aware of the situation. "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday, but said he hadn't spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it yet. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." The Department of Health and Human Services and the State Department are also monitoring the situation. What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia Tuesday to share more information about Shipilova's death, per Reuters . ​Rubio told reporters: "I ​think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously ⁠share more information with the world." Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

events.title: Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says
events.summary: The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading US AI model makers, is no contest when it comes to assessing which one gives you more value for your subscription money, according to industry research firm SemiAnalysis. Following changes to OpenAI's $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that's still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services. AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates. And SemiAnalysis argues that it's necessary to delve into subscription pricing to evaluate AI shops financially because subscription usage consumes a disproportionate amount of company compute resources. Claude subscriptions, the biz claims, take up about 42 percent of Anthropic's inference compute while generating just 10 percent of its revenue. And those subscriptions provide considerable value. "Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board," SemiAnalysis claims in reference to mid-tier models GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. "You could argue that this is unfair for [OpenAI] because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens." OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. SemiAnalysis' calculation relies on measuring token output rates, converting those into tokens per 5-hour usage window and per month, and then computing the API-equivalent value. Company researchers contend that API-equivalent value is the best figure for capturing the value of a subscription plan, though they allow that other measures like raw token volume may be more appropriate in some instances. API-based comparisons can be slow to account for the rapidly shifting capabilities of models that come to market. The debut of a new open source model, for example, can alter what's possible at a given price. For those with access to subscription plans, the subsidized prices clearly offer real value, so much so that there's an underground market for reselling tokens from pooled subscription accounts in many parts of the world. But there are other ways to measure AI value. Artificial Analysis, for example, tracks cost per task – the estimated dollar cost of completing a specific task. By that yardstick, GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72) is far more affordable than Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98), at least for those paying API rates. But that ratio may not be true for different tasks – benchmark performance may not reflect your workload. As measured by tokens, Claude Pro ($20 per month) provides 2.9 billion tokens per month, compared to ChatGPT ($20/mo) at 1 billion tokens per month, according to SemiAnalysis. But models may use more or fewer tokens than others for the same task, and when the output is functional, like code, AI output may achieve a similar result across different models but with differing degrees of efficiency. Anticipating AI costs gets more complicated for businesses, which can't count on subscription subsidies and may not have experience with AI cost management. In a July report, McKinsey said 93 percent of enterprises exceeded their AI budgets. "I think all businesses are seeing their AI costs rise," said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of AI agent biz Skydive, in an interview with The Register. Since the beginning of the year, he said, AI has been getting better at solving certain business problems, and companies have started deploying AI more widely, then noticing their token bills going through the roof. "The labs typically subsidize their prosumer plans with subscription pricing massively," said Amin. "And I think it's part of their marketing funnel because more people are able to use the tools, get familiar with the tools, and then bring those tools to work." But for larger companies, he said, two problems arise. You have more employees than can fit on a subsidized plan and, at scale, costs add up fast. "A huge way that enterprises solve this is being able to make a workload work well on the frontier and then quickly switch it to an open source model that they control and that they can serve at a much lower fraction of the cost," he said. "And so for us internally we were able to drop our AI costs 75 percent plus just by moving them all to Skydive Glide, which is our model router that for the given workload tries to find an equivalent open source model that can handle that workload without a quality drop. And so today we run a lot of our workloads on GLM-5.3 Flash." Amin said that companies adept at AI cost management maintain evaluation benchmarks that reflect their workloads. Companies use those metrics to test new models as they come out in whatever AI harness they're using, to ensure consistency. Looking ahead, he said, he expects companies will trust more of that work to service providers. "So what this means is that if you deploy an agent on top of us, we capture in the background the data of how that agent's actually running in production," he said. "And then we use that to construct the eval data set on the fly." ® Updated Oct 6 at 2322 GMT to clarify that Skydive is the platform that sells the agents, while Anything is the umbrella parent company.

events.title: Programmable Memory Controller Eases Adoption of New DRAM Techniques (ETH Zürich, CISPA, NYU)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at ETH Zürich, CISPA , and New York University published a technical paper titled “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.” “DRAM continues to limit the performance, energy efficiency, and robustness of modern systems. Many prior works propose DRAM techniques that support in-DRAM computation, improve memory access latency and parallelism, and enhance DRAM maintenance and reliability. However, adopting each new technique requires repeated modifications to the rigid DRAM interface and memory controller, hindering its deployment. Our goal is to reduce these repeated modifications. We observe that the DRAM commands and memory controller structures of many DRAM techniques are similar. Our key idea is to use these similarities to compose a set of primitives for implementing diverse DRAM techniques. We propose Terracotta, a new framework with two flexible components: (i) custom command extensions that let DRAM vendors define new commands within a single, standardized interface, and (ii) a programmable memory controller that system designers can program to support new DRAM techniques post-silicon. Together, these enable deployment by configuring the memory controller instead of modifying the interface and controller. ” Find the technical paper here . October 2026. events.title: A brutal winter heating bill is coming for some homes
events.summary: Americans could pay far more to heat their homes with oil this winter than last, a new analysis reviewed by Axios shows, as volatile energy markets and the Iran War deepen the affordability crisis. Why it matters: Heating bills are eating into household budgets before winter sets in, with stark divides between fuel types. By the numbers: Families that heat with oil could pay about 50% more this winter than last, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), up from its 31.3% projection in mid-September. The average cost of heating a home with oil is expected to rise by about $878, costing over $2,600 this winter. By comparison, the Energy Information Administration's Winter Fuels Outlook released Tuesday projects electricity bills will rise 4% nationally, while natural gas bills will fall 9% and propane spending will drop 3%. EIA expects a smaller increase on heating oil than NEADA, projecting a 21% increase in household expenditures. Northeastern households will feel the pain most acutely: about 82% of home heating oil is consumed in the region, where some states lack robust natural gas pipelines, according to NEADA data. Just 3% of U.S. households use oil as their primary heat source, compared to about 45% using natural gas and 43% using electricity, NEADA says. The big picture: Heating oil prices are rising as global oil markets falter because of the wars in Iran and Ukraine and as refinery activity declines. "Those trends really reflect the worst-case scenario of this war, and they are going to feel it this winter, and it's unfortunate," Mark Wolfe, executive director of the NEADA, tells Axios. What they're saying: Because of the cost, some families will cut back on food or medicine, borrow from payday lenders, or turn the heat down to unsafe levels to cover their heating bills, Wolfe says. " With low-income families, sometimes states will move money around to help them, but they'll go without, " Wolfe says. Between the lines: States can put more money toward heating assistance, but they have fewer tools to protect heating-oil customers than households served by regulated gas and electric utilities, Wolfe says. States can require utilities to offer discounts, affordability programs or winter shutoff protections, but they generally don't apply to independent heating-oil dealers. Zoom in: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey declared a State of Energy Emergency Monday over rising winter energy costs, unlocking nearly $150 million in relief and expanding assistance to middle-class households that heat with oil. Rhode Island has also declared an energy affordability emergency and directed $28 million in reserves toward winter electric-bill relief, and Maine Gov. Janet Mills announced $40 million in automatically applied electricity discounts for low-income residents. Zoom out: The energy affordability crisis is compounded by the Trump administration's attempts to dismantle the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP. The administration fired LIHEAP's federal staff at the Department of Health and Human Services in April 2025 and proposed eliminating funding for the program. LIHEAP is still running, but state administrators are operating without dedicated federal staff. The White House referred Axios to HHS, which said it "will carry out its responsibilities for funding Congress has made available" and that "HHS has the staff and capacity to distribute these funds in a timely manner." The bottom line: Winter is coming, and Americans need to prepare for both the cold — and the prices — to bite. Go deeper: How to save money on your electric bill this winter

India's central bank lifted rates by 25 bps for the first time in nearly four years amid rising inflation and strong economic growth. See how the day unfolded on the ABC's business and markets blog. Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice. The ASX200 had a strange day , where it rose higher, then sank, then rose again, before finally settling just below yesterday's close . Companies linked with uranium mining or enrichment such as Deep Yellow, Silex Systems, Paladin Energy and NexGen Energy had a good day after Google signed a huge energy deal with Constellation Energy in the US which will lead to more demand for nuclear energy. India's central bank lifted interest rates by 25 bps for the first time in nearly four years amid mounting inflation. It has joined other central banks in raising rates as higher oil prices triggered by the Iran war fuel inflation globally. We'll be back early tomorrow morning to catch you up on developments in global markets overnight. Until then, take care of yourselves. The best performing stocks on the ASX200 were Arena Reit ( +12.98% ) and Deep Yellow ( +4.61% ). The two worst performing stocks in the index were Elsight Ltd (-5.57%) and Sims Limited (-4.78% ). Trading has finished on Australia's stock market for the day. The S & P/ASX200 index closed down just 8 points ( -0.09% ) to 8,727 points. Ten Cap portfolio manager steering clear of Firmus IPO The ABC's chief business correspondent Ian Verrender wrote a fascinating article on the weekend about Firmus Technologies , an AI data centre builder and operator. Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion in an initial public offering this month and is scheduled to start trading on the ASX on 23 October . But Ten Cap portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu is steering clear of the IPO, citing unprecedented lack of disclosure and enormous structural risks. Here's what she says in a note that's being circulated today: "Firmus is probably one of the most polarising IPOs I have ever seen. The lack of detail they disclose is unprecedented. "I think Firmus is a very high-risk proposition — very high profile, but with enormous risk involved. "97% of the data centre capacity they've promised hasn't even been built. They might deliver cheaper earnings in two years if they build what they promise, but that's speculative. "If you want data centre exposure you've got NextDC (ASX:NCT) and Goodman Group. Both are better operators with proven track records. "We much prefer to be in the companies that actually build those data centres — the engineers, the electrical contractors like Southern Cross Electrical (ASX: SXE) and Genusplus (ASX:GNP). "There are a lot of those smaller businesses now benefiting from the huge buildout that Australia is about to see.” Recently retired RBA board member says another rate rise this year is 'plausible' I attended a fascinating discussion at the Centre for Independent Studies , where its CEO and former AFR editor Michael Stutchbury was in conversation with former RBA Monetary Policy Board member Ian Harper . Harper only left the board after the bank's August meeting, where it left rates on hold, and was not present for the September meeting where it unanimously decided to raise the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6%. He didn't want to second guess the board's deliberations in September, nor offer a view on the likely level of interest rates going forward. But he, like the RBA governor at her post-meeting press conference, wouldn't rule out the potential for another rate hike this year. " The bank moving again before the end of the year is plausible , from what I can see of the circumstances," Harper told the lunchtime audience. "But, again, I don't have the [board] papers in front of me." Ian Harper made some time after his speech to sit down for a one-on-one interview with David Taylor , which you can watch on The Business tonight at 8:44pm AEDT or catch up any time on iview or the program page.

events.title: Permanent daylight saving time could be a public health time bomb
events.summary: President Trump is pushing hard for the US Senate to make daylight saving time permanent so, among other things, golfers can stay on the course longer, but it may not be such a bright idea. New research out of Canada suggests that, even if Americans would get an extra hour of daylight in the evening, the ill health effects of permanent daylight saving time could outweigh the benefits. A paper published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on Monday reviewed evidence on the health effects of permanent daylight saving time (pDST) as several Canadian jurisdictions move to stop changing their clocks. It finds that the opposite approach - adoption of permanent standard time (pST) - would actually be better for people’s health. Sorry, night owls and after-work social butterflies, but the science simply isn’t with you on this one. “Permanent DST preserves later evening light that may facilitate commuting, recreation, social participation, and some economic activity, but it also prolongs darkness on winter mornings,” the authors note. Prolonged morning darkness doesn't really jibe with the inner workings of the human body and light’s essential role in regulating the circadian rhythm. Sure, no one wants to drive home from work in the dark, but we really need morning light to get us functioning properly. Our circadian rhythms, the authors explain, actually run on a slightly longer schedule than a full day - 24.2 hours. For that reason, we rely on natural sunlight to keep us synchronized with the world around us. Morning light is some of the most important, the authors note, because it jump starts that rhythm, wakes us up and gets us moving. Evening light, on the other hand, delays the circadian rhythm, messing with our sense of “social time” and making it tougher to get to sleep and wake up rested in the morning. The effects of later evening light can show up in sleep, mood, education, and work productivity, the authors noted, and we don’t even need pDST to see some of those associations - we can just look at time zones. Move from east to west in the US or Canada and you’ll get some considerable differences in when the sun rises and sets in a particular time zone - in some cases, sunrise and sunset can differ by more than an hour of clock time across a single time zone. In one study cited by the Canadian analysis, residents on the western side of US time zones, where the sun sets later, got around an hour less sleep a week. The study also estimated that an additional hour of sleep per week was associated with around 5 percent higher long-term earnings. Similar results turned up in a German study, the team noted. Another study found that workers on the western end of US time zones ended up working fewer hours, too. On the educational front, an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores in a Florida study “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions.” “Ending biannual clock adjustments may eliminate transition harms that last a few weeks, but the health effects of permanent time are likely to be chronic,” the authors noted. “The preponderance of health evidence favors pST, which would align with the recommendations of sleep and chronobiology societies worldwide.” This isn’t the first time researchers have concluded such. British sleep scientists concluded much the same in 2024, which led to their recommendation to permanently kill DST in favor of a permanent shift to Greenwich Mean Time. That isn’t stopping the US from plowing ahead with plans for pDST, though. The Senate passed a measure to enshrine DST in 2022, but the House never acted on it. This time around, the House has passed its own bill to enact pDST, but the Senate is dithering, leading President Trump to go so far as to post the personal cellphone number of one Republican holdout on social media, Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR), who is opposed to the measure. “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton explained in a post on X following Trump’s doxxing. He’s right, too: The US has twice enacted pDST - once during World War II, which ended after the war, and again in 1973 as an energy saving measure. Congress curtailed the experiment later in 1974 following public backlash over dark winter mornings. The US isn’t alone in trying and failing at enacting pDST, either, as the Canadian paper points out. Russia adopted pDST in 2011 and reversed it in 2014. Chile tried and reversed it as well. In those cases, the reasons for reversing course varied, but concerns included dark winter mornings, disrupted sleep and body clocks, safety, and public dissatisfaction. It’s unclear whether the US government’s latest attempt at enacting pDST will succeed despite political resistance and scientific evidence that it’s a bad idea, but the researchers sure seem to hope not: They note that, if the US makes such a change, Canada will likely be pressured to conform. At the end of the day, we might all be better off just dealing with a couple of clock changes and some short-term sleep disruption. ®

events.title: Texan company plans to build new outback town for gas workers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Dunmarra Development Land plans to build village in remote NT for gas workers A digital render of a 120-unit cluster in the planned village, called Dunmarra, in the remote NT. ( Supplied: Dunmarra Development Land ) Dunmarra Development Land has published plans to build a 600 hectare "petroleum services precinct and workforce village" near the Beetaloo Basin. It would house up to 3,000 workers and provide a range of services which could be used by the public. It is understood no planning or environmental applications have been made at this stage. A Texan company has plans for a new "workforce village", which could house up to 3,000 gas workers in a remote part of the Northern Territory. Dunmarra Development Land has published plans online, which say thousands of people could be housed at its 600 hectare "petroleum services precinct and workforce village". It would be located just south of the Dunmarra Wayside Inn in Birdum, about 600 kilometres south of Darwin, and include supermarkets, a medical clinic, airstrip and sporting facilities, with all open for public use. At full capacity it would provide 23 unit complexes as accommodation for a "rotating workforce", with services provided in the "town centre". A worker at Tamboran's Beetaloo site, which recently started supplying gas to the energy grid. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Drilling companies and gas industry contractors would also be able to lease commercial lots to base their business operations at the precinct. The website does not state how much construction would cost or how long it would take to build, but it does say it would not be permanent. Dunmarra is close to the Beetaloo Basin, a massive gas resource which the industry and NT government say could provide a long-term gas supply for energy markets both domestically and overseas . The company is owned by Kit Sheffield, a relative and business associate of Bryan Sheffield, an American businessman who invested in Tamboran Resources's project in the Beetaloo, which recently produced its first gas . "Gas development in the Beetaloo brings drilling, completions, civil and logistics crews to a region with almost no serviced land and no workforce housing," the website said. "Dunmarra puts the workshop, the bed and the mess in one place, on the highway, with gas and an airstrip at the fence." If fully built, the development would be one of the biggest settlements in the NT and dwarf pre-existing towns in the area such as Elliott, Daly Waters and remote communities. Kit Sheffield was contacted for comment. Barkly Regional Council Mayor Sid Vashist said he was unaware of the plan before he was contacted by the ABC. Sid Vashist says local government has not been contacted about the plan. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) He said it was important the development supported existing towns in the region like Elliott and did not reinforce the industry's reliance on fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workforces. "This is literally a huge township that's going to be proposed and created, which could be bigger than Tennant Creek at this stage," Cr Vashist said. He said it was important to have long-term plans for developments built due to the resources sector to ensure they thrive after the lucrative industry departs. "Towns like Tennant Creek were built on mines, but when the mining left, the socio-economic profile of the residents in this town reduced quite significantly, which has been a huge challenge," he said. It is understood no environmental or development applications have been lodged with the NT government.

events.title: Google backs 'existing nuclear plants' as data centres strain US energy grid
events.summary: Google has said that its data centre growth , fuelled by the artificial intelligence boom, led the company to reach a power-purchase agreement involving the upgrade of six nuclear plants in the US. An essay posted to Google's corporate news detailed the agreement made with Constellation , which operates the "largest fleet of nuclear facilities in the US". Through the PPA, Google says it is essentially enabling more than "1.5GW of new nuclear capacity for the US energy system from increasing the power output of existing reactors and bringing dormant facilities back online". Technology companies continue to come under criticism in the US over the rise in data centre construction. The centres cause energy demand to surge in some areas and lead to an increase in electricity prices for consumers. "As our data centre investments in the US continue, so does our commitment to revitalise the nation’s energy supply, support local jobs and economic opportunity, and bring new reliable electricity capacity to strengthen US grids at no cost to other ratepayers," Google said. The company said that as part of the PPA, Constellation had agreed to use the technology company's agentic AI "workflows across its core operations to accelerate uprate planning, streamline construction and optimise plant output". Nuclear criticism Google is the latest among Big Tech firms to support nuclear reactors in the US, although the moves have not always been welcomed. Critics say that many of the reactor deals include large loans from the US government, meaning citizens are paying for nuclear energy centres. On Monday, the US Department of Energy announced the latest such deal "of up to $4.2 billion" to modernise nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania. "By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, round-the-clock energy for American families and businesses," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. There are also concerns about safety. Constellation's PPA with Microsoft in 2024 involved the rehabilitation of one of the Three Mile Island reactors in Middletown, Pennsylvania. In March 1979, the core of TMI Unit 2 was partially exposed, prompting a temporary partial evacuation of the area and a lengthy clean-up around Middletown that continues to this day. Although it is Unit 1 of TMI, closed in 2019, that is being rehabilitated, energy safety groups have continued to express concern. And in Covert, Michigan, efforts to restart the Palisades nuclear reactor, which closed in 2022, are also under way. The owners of Palisades, Holtec International , had hoped to restart the reactor by this year, but a series of incidents have cast doubt on that goal. In September, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission confirmed that it was investigating an incident related to a "tipped fuel assembly" that occurred while the reactor was being fuelled. On Tuesday, however, Google did not appear concerned about the potential for opposition as it promoted its endeavour with Constellation. "This builds a more affordable energy future for everyone," the company said. It said it was providing guaranteed revenue that Constellation "needs to invest in upgrades for 11 of their nuclear reactors, while ensuring other grid customers bear none of the associated costs".

events.title: Singles tax costs thousands of dollars a year
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Singles struggle to afford housing as cost of living rises Louise Taylor faced affordability issues when looking for somewhere to call home. ( ABC News: Lottie Twyford ) Single-income households can struggle to meet housing costs, and older women are one group at risk of housing insecurity. The singles tax refers to extra costs people pay when they can't split expenses like couples can. Housing experts say Australia also has a lack of affordable, suitable dwellings for singles. By her 70s, Louise Taylor had hoped her house would be more than a roof over her head; somewhere she could happily call home. But after "knockback after knockback" trying to find a rental on the private market five years ago, she has been forced to accept her small duplex, north of Brisbane, is all she can afford. "I was at desperate times and I went, 'You know what, I don't care, I just have to do it'," she says. "I was so grateful … then I'm looking around thinking, 'Where am I going to put my lounge room?'" Ms Taylor is the first to acknowledge she is one of the lucky ones and is currently on the housing waitlist. She has also contacted other housing organisations to see if they can help. Louise Taylor is living in a modest duplex north of Brisbane. ( ABC News ) On the pension, she fears the next rent rise and that, if it gets any more expensive, she believes she will have no choice but to move in with her adult daughter. She is also scared that if she cannot afford to rent a house on her own, she may have no choice but to move into a share house. Ms Taylor believes she would have had more success finding a rental, and more power on the private rental market, if she had been applying in a couple. Singles tax costing people hundreds of dollars a month That concept is known as the singles tax — the idea that single-income households do not enjoy the same cost-sharing benefits when it comes to things such as rent and bills as a couple does. Australian Bureau of Statistics data suggests a single person spends more than $770 extra on living costs a month compared to a person in a couple. Better Financial Planning's Michael Khouri says a single person also has to take on more of the mental load managing finances. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Brisbane financial adviser Michael Khouri said there was also the time and effort factor to consider, as well as that inability to share resources. "If somebody's single and they're trying to do everything themselves, they're usually a bit more time-poor," he said. He said he also sees people who have just come out of a separation struggling to fund separate homes — either renting or buying — especially as the cost of housing continues to rise. "Fifteen years ago, I'd find that probably half or maybe, say, 30 to 40 per cent of their expenses was housing, and now it's just getting higher and higher." Louise Taylor says her two-bedroom duplex is more like a one-bedroom home. ( ABC News ) More than half of Australians living alone are women, and about half of those women are 65 or older. Older women are also a growing group at risk of experiencing housing distress or homelessness. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reports that women and girls make up 60 per cent of the people seeking assistance from homelessness services. And the number of homeless women over 55 has surged, with earlier census data pointing to an approximately 40 per cent increase over the decade from 2011 . Single, older women at risk of housing insecurity Maggie Shambrook says many older women are reluctant to describe themselves as homeless. ( ABC News: Elizabeth Pickering ) The Housing Older Women Movement's Maggie Shambrook said many women who fell into that cohort were living invisibly — couch-surfing or living in vans as they searched for an affordable, suitable home. Some empty-nesters want to move into smaller homes but say the cost of doing so keeps them in their large properties. Ms Shambrook said systemic issues including having worked in lower-paid professions or participated in unpaid caring work, along with the difficulty of building an asset base, contributed to this. And as Ms Taylor had experienced, there was also the issue of finding something suitable and affordable for a single person, especially as they aged. "Your mobility does change as you get older … your ability to navigate obstacles becomes less and less," Ms Shambrook said. "Mould, poor fittings and, in hot weather, no good ventilation, that's a serious issue.

"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," he wrote, referring to a super PAC affiliated with the president. Nonetheless, one such ad repurposes a nearly identical ad from Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, cutting it shorter and adding "Paid for by the U.S. government." events.title: Hackers obtain counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large services
events.summary: Attackers hijacked three top-level domains and used their control to mint counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large organizations, Google said Tuesday. The attackers launched a series of attacks on the .gh, .sl, and .as country code top-level domains (ccTLDs) and then modified authoritative DNS records for selected domains within those namespaces. By controlling those DNS records, the attackers were able to pass automated domain control validation checks and obtain unauthorized certificates for “several Google domains” and “several leading global brands and widely used online services.” Google said it updated Chrome to block all certificates it identified as unauthorized, and worked with the issuing certification authorities to ensure the unauthorized certificates for Google properties were revoked. Certificate issuance: The weak link in the chain TLS certificates are the cryptographic credentials that underpin authentication and encryption protections for websites, mail servers, and other Internet infrastructure. These x.509 certificates use a digital signature to bind a domain name such as google.com to a public key. The public key is publicly available, while the private key is held only by the website operator. When a connection shows that the keys match, the visiting party knows it’s connected to the authentic site rather than an impostor. Possession of unauthorized certificates allows attackers to cryptographically impersonate the affected infrastructure. Read full article Comments

events.title: From research to real-world value
events.summary: A*Star is helping businesses turn innovation into stronger capabilities, greater productivity and new opportunities – creating value that extends well beyond the laboratory An AI-powered vision system, co-developed by Sunningdale Tech and A*Star, inspects components on the factory floor. Singapore’s sustained investment in research and development is not only building scientific capabilities, but also delivering value today through stronger companies, new businesses, intellectual property, quality jobs and capabilities that help Singapore remain competitive in a rapidly changing global economy. These outcomes are the result of partnerships and engagements that deepen over years, rather than one-off projects. The impact can be seen in two very different journeys: one helps an established manufacturer move up the technology curve, and another that has taken Singapore-developed research from the lab to global markets. Sunningdale Tech, an established precision engineering and manufacturing company, has worked with A*Star to adopt artificial intelligence, robotics and automation. The collaboration has improved the company’s productivity and quality while strengthening its Singapore-based capabilities to fuel its global operations. Respiree represents another pathway. Spun off from research at A*Star, the medtech company has developed research in optical sensing and biophotonics into an AI-enabled platform for continuous cardio-respiratory monitoring. The stories of Sunningdale and Respiree demonstrate A*Star’s role in connecting research capabilities with industry needs and translating science into products, businesses and capabilities. “Being a bridge means closing the gap between scientific discovery and real-world adoption,” says Beh Kian Teik, chief executive, A*Star. “As Singapore’s innovation ecosystem matures, our role is evolving too. It is no longer simply about transferring a technology from the lab to a company. Increasingly, we help bring together the research, infrastructure, talent, industry partners and capital needed to move an idea towards deployment.” Rather than treating commercialisation as a linear process, A*Star is building what Beh calls “more repeatable pathways from research to real-world use”. For Sunningdale Tech, the starting point was a practical manufacturing challenge. One example was the inspection of impeller components, where even a small cosmetic flaw could affect performance. Operators were carrying out manual inspections around the clock, checking about 10,000 parts a day. Conventional machine vision systems were not flexible enough and every new product required manual reprogramming. The company needed a system that could identify genuine defects across different product variants and moulds while accounting for variables such as reflections and lighting. That led Sunningdale to A*Star, with which it has worked since 2021. “We have seen how much AI capability they have built up over the years through their research,” says Barry Tay, senior director, Sunningdale Innovation Tech Centre. “So when this specific gap came up, they were the obvious partner to help us close it, leveraging on A*Star’s deep technical expertise in machine learning and computer vision.” Barry Tay, senior director, Sunningdale Innovation Tech Centre. Sunningdale engineers developed the system needed to present each component correctly to the cameras, while researchers at A*Star trained the algorithm to distinguish genuine defects from normal variations. One product alone had six different moulds, and the algorithm needed to work reliably across all of them. Early versions were too sensitive, identifying imperfections that human inspectors would not consider defects and resulting in excessive rejection rates. “It took months of back-and-forth to calibrate it properly, so it matched what our customers actually consider acceptable, not some theoretical perfect standard,” Tay says. A*Star’s involvement has extended beyond individual projects. Through the Technology for Enterprise Capability Upgrading (T-UP) programme, its engineers have worked alongside Sunningdale’s teams on practical manufacturing challenges, with a seconded A*Star engineer instrumental in its wider push towards Industry 5.0 and automation. The AI inspection project has similarly built Sunningdale’s AI and computer-vision capabilities. Once fully deployed, it will increase inspection capacity from about 10,000 to up to 30,000 components a day and generate hundreds of thousands of dollars in annual savings, while freeing operators for higher-value work. The framework could eventually be deployed across Sunningdale’s 21 sites in 11 countries, extending a solution co-developed in Singapore with A*Star’s engineering talent to its global operations. Several multinational customers have already expressed interest in applying the capability to future production lines, strengthening Sunningdale’s position as a more advanced manufacturing partner.

events.title: I’ve Covered Death Row Cases for Nearly a Decade. What Happened to Christa Pike Wasn’t an Anomaly.
events.summary: The death chamber in Huntsville, Texas Joe Raedle/Getty Images Over the course of two hours, witnesses watched and listened as Christa Pike cried, whimpered and snored through Tennessee’s attempt to execute her. By the end of it, executioners had given her two doses of the state’s lethal injection drugs. Her arms were swollen and blistered, and one had turned purple, her attorneys said. And she was still alive, marking what legal experts say is the first time a prisoner in the U.S. has survived one dose — let alone two — of lethal injection drugs.  Even if the outcome was unprecedented, what went wrong was not. Pike’s was the third Tennessee execution in 14 months to go awry. But as a reporter who has covered death row for nearly a decade and witnessed several executions, I know the state is not alone. The factors behind the breakdowns in Tennessee have popped up again and again across the country — and show how easily another botched execution could occur, even as soon as the ones planned Wednesday in Texas and next week in Florida. Here’s what we know about Tennessee’s attempt to execute Pike: The procedure started more than nine hours late, delayed by last-minute legal fights. Then, inside the death house, executioners struggled to find a vein, jabbing Pike with at least seven needles, according to her lawyers, one of whom watched in dismay. As the caustic barbiturate finally started flowing into the IV lines, Pike did not fall into sedation quickly. Instead, witnesses said, she sang with her spiritual adviser. Then she said her arm felt like it was about to burst open. “Does this happen like that?” she asked.  Like Pike, many aging death row prisoners have medical problems that can complicate efforts to kill them, potentially turning what are supposed to be relatively quick deaths into agonizing, drawn-out procedures. Even when prisoners are healthy, several states have faced questions about the competence of their execution teams, as both the American Medical Association and American Nurses Association have strongly opposed their members taking part in death penalty procedures. And death penalty states across the country shroud their executions in such secrecy that it is often difficult or impossible to confirm the age, source or sterility of the drugs. “The types of failures that went into this botch happen all the time,” said Robert Dunham, director of the Death Penalty Policy Project. “There is nothing in the execution process that states are incapable of getting wrong.” The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment, though hours after the attempted execution the agency said in a statement that it had “followed every step” of the state’s established protocol, which “has been consistently effective.” On Saturday, the head of the agency resigned . Meanwhile, Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he had ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the execution previously scheduled for December would no longer take place this year. His office didn’t respond to a request for comment. On Friday, Pike’s lawyers filed a motion asking a court to order the agency to preserve any evidence related to the state’s failed effort to kill their client. In a statement, they said the filing “details the serious complications that occurred during the execution attempt, many of which Christa and her attorneys had warned the State and the courts about months earlier.” Pike remains in the hospital where she is receiving critical medical care, they said. After several days on a ventilator, intubated and unconscious, on Tuesday afternoon her attorneys said she was awake and speaking. “Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” they wrote in a statement. “We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.” Unhealthy Prisoners By the time the Tennessee Department of Correction strapped her to the gurney last week, Pike had been on death row for 30 years. She had been sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer , a fellow Job Corps student in Knoxville. Pike was 18 at the time and, like many people on death row , had a history of mental illness and childhood sexual abuse .  Now 50 years old, Pike has faced an array of health problems, which her legal team had repeatedly warned could lead to a bungled execution. During a three-day hearing in August , Pike’s attorneys argued that her small veins and a blood disorder would make it harder and more painful to put in the IV lines to administer the lethal dose. The Tennessee Supreme Court did not agree , calling their arguments “speculative” and rejecting their request for a stay. Tennessee’s execution protocol relies on pentobarbital, a caustic barbiturate that slows down breathing and has been used to treat seizures, sedate people before surgery and euthanize animals. But its use in putting to death humans has drawn scrutiny. After relying on the drug for all 13 federal executions during the first Trump administration, the Justice Department under President Joe Biden said there was too much uncertainty about whether it would cause “ unnecessary pain and suffering ” and decided to stop using it “unless and until that uncertainty is resolved.” This year, President Donald Trump’s DOJ reversed course and readopted its use. Despite supply difficulties and repeated lawsuits from death row prisoners arguing that using pentobarbital is cruel and unusual, several states still use it, including Georgia, Missouri, South Carolina and Texas, where I witnessed five executions in the late 2010s as a reporter for the Houston Chronicle. Four of the condemned prisoners said the drug burned. Two said they could taste it. One said he could “hear it going through the vein.” But all of them stopped moving within minutes and were declared dead in under an hour.  Tennessee prison officials have not offered an explanation as to why Pike’s attempted execution was so drastically different. Initially, Pike’s attorneys and several death penalty experts raised the possibility that the drugs may have been too old or degraded to work as intended. Yet in Friday’s legal filings, Pike’s lawyers focused on the way the drug was administered, saying it was “abundantly clear” that Tennessee prison officials either didn’t know that the IV lines were out of place or didn’t realize her veins had been so badly damaged that the highly alkaline liquid started leaking out into the surrounding tissue of her arm. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta and one of Pike’s medical experts , said that meant there wasn’t enough of the drug in her bloodstream at once to kill her. “It just got into her arms, and most of it stopped there,” he said.   Like Pike, many people on death rows nationwide have significant health problems often compounded by old

events.title: DOJ moves to strip citizenship from 40 people
events.summary: President Trump's Justice Department moved to revoke citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in recent months, representing what Attorney General Todd Blanche called the "largest denaturalization effort in modern history." The big picture: The Trump administration has made denaturalization a priority, moving personnel to pursue more cases and setting a goal of 250 cases by this month. Driving the news: The DOJ filed 40 denaturalization actions in district courts spanning coast to coast between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2, according to a Monday statement . "Every single one of these individuals lied their way into U.S. citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement. Context: Denaturalization cases have a high burden of proof, and to revoke someone's citizenship, the DOJ must file a revocation action in federal district court. The general grounds for revocation, per U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, are illegal procurement of naturalized citizenship or lying to get it. "For civil revocation of naturalization, the burden of proof is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence which does not leave the issue in doubt," per USCIS. Zoom in: Individuals named in Monday's statement had been convicted of or pleaded guilty to an array of offenses, including conspiracy to commit money laundering, sexual abuse of a minor and aggravated sodomy. What we're watching: The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for specifics on how many actions had been filed since the start of the second Trump administration. In April, the New York Times reported that the DOJ had identified 384 foreign-born Americans whose citizenship the department wanted to revoke. The following month, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported that USCIS lawyers had been temporarily moved to U.S. attorneys' offices to work on denaturalization cases. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Oh lawd it is coming ... to Hugging Face later this month AMD bets $8.2B that worlds matter more than words in AI 8 days ago French dev aims to solve bots' blindness so they can understand GUIs 8 days ago Dutch government turns to NixOS for a sovereign desktop 9 days ago DeepSeek's new model sets a template for powerful LLMs that run lean 26 days ago The search company that plants trees just launched a Linux browser to help Europe battle big tech September 4, 2026 Another week brings yet another open weights model and this one is huge — or at least it is for Europe's AI flag bearer Mistral, which has taken to calling the 1 trillion-parameter large language model (LLM) Le Chonk. Its product name is Mistral Large 4 , which is a lot less fun than the cat-meme-inspired "very official" moniker Le Chonk. Nonetheless, the LLM is the French model-dev's biggest open weights release ever. At a trillion parameters, Le Chonk is squarely in frontier territory, and like most modern frontier models, it is multimodal, reasoning, and employs a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture with about 49 billion active parameters to keep serving costs low. Mistral didn't offer any guidance on hardware requirements in its release blog, but the model is still small enough to run reasonably on 8-way GPU boxes like Nvidia's HGX B300 or AMD's MI355X. We know far more about the hardware the model was trained on. According to Mistral, this Chonker was trained using roughly 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs — or around 52 NVL72 racks — in Mistral's own datacenters located in Europe on a corpus spanning more than 160 languages using a combination of supervised pre-training and reinforcement learning. Sovereign AI remains a major focus for Europe and Mistral is clearly cashing in on demand for frontier class models trained and run within Europe's borders. The model itself is currently in preview, but you won't have to wait long for its weights to drop. Mistral expects them to be live on Hugging Face and other model repos within the month. Early testing by independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis puts Le Chonk at a major disadvantage relative to OpenAI or Anthropic's flagship models. In the AI guru's intelligence leaderboard, Mistral Large 4 preview sits between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenAI's entry-level GPT6 Luna models. Having said that, Mistral's latest model outshines the United States' most capable open weights model, Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling , by a significant margin. So when it comes to non-Chinese LLMs you can actually download, Mistral does quite well. As you'd expect, Mistral's own benchmarks tell a far rosier story. Across coding, agentic, finance, and legal benchmarks, the model build shows its latest LLM trading blows with some of the top Chinese offerings from Alibaba, Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek. You can find their charts here , but as always take them with a grain of salt. One area Mistral is particularly proud of is Le Chonk's performance in cybersecurity workloads. The company claims the model is one of the strongest performers in cybersecurity benchmarks like Artificial Analysis' new Cyber inde x. This is a dig at proprietary American models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which have a tendency to refuse cybersecurity-related tasks that could be perceived as adversarial. As we previously reported , this is potentially problematic for customers trying to use AI models to red-team their own systems in order to identify vulnerabilities before someone else finds them. "Provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies," Mistral wrote in a blog post .

events.title: AI tools flood into underground cybercrime markets
events.summary: Hackers in underground cybercriminal forums are on shopping sprees for new AI tools , according to research shared first with Axios. Why it matters: AI is making once-specialized hacking capabilities cheaper and easier to buy, potentially transforming far more criminals into dangerous hackers. By the numbers: Advertisements for AI tools on underground forums and platforms surged from fewer than 50 per month in late 2025 to more than 1,400 by February, according to a report from Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center. Sellers offered access to ChatGPT Plus accounts for as little as 10 cents and jailbreak prompts to trick models into breaking their safeguards for 32 cents, per the research. Halcyon studied nearly 4,000 posts across 77 Telegram channels, 20 dark web forums and five specialized underground markets between October and May. Threat level: Companies are already losing millions of dollars to the types of cyberattacks enabled by the tools found on these underground markets. "It really goes to show you how cheap it is to conduct these activities ... which should be scary for organizations," Cynthia Kaiser, head of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of FBI Cyber, told Axios. The big picture: Cybercriminals have completely commercialized the sale and creation of these tools, often modeling software-as-a-service subscription models and online storefronts, per the report. Some sellers are now offering AI tools they tested and promoted on traditional dark web forums through easier-to-manage storefronts hosted on Telegram. "It shouldn't have been shocking to me," Kaiser said. "But what we should take away from this is also how much cybercriminals have learned throughout the years about how to sell and package — and they applied this really quickly to the AI models." Zoom in: Hackers are selling four types of AI tools: Jailbroken and stolen AI services, including prompts that allow users to strip the safety guardrails from mainstream models for as little as $10. Identity fraud and phishing tools that make impersonating real people quick and easy. Access to models trained on malicious data to aid cybercrime, such as the popular WormGPT that's designed to write phishing emails and malware. AI-augmented malware and infrastructure, including a system that can call as many as 120 people at once as part of a scam operation. Flashback: In 2023, hackers could only tap a handful of one-off tools. Now, there's a robust marketplace. Still, AI is largely helping criminals perform discrete elements of existing attacks more cheaply and efficiently, Kaiser said. "What you're not seeing for sale is an agent that does it all for you and has this amazing success rate," she said. What to watch: Halcyon didn't find evidence of criminals selling AI systems capable of running fully autonomous cyberattacks. Even in AI-enabled malware and infrastructure, Kaiser said, much of what researchers are seeing involves coding assistance, infrastructure and other individual tasks rather than AI creating and deploying malware on its own. events.title: Paramount closes historic $110B deal for Warner Bros. Discovery to create Skydance
events.summary: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday closed its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, ending a dramatic, yearlong process that rattled Hollywood, Wall Street and Washington. Why it matters: The deal creates one of the largest entertainment behemoths in the world and makes David Ellison — a lesser-known figure outside of Hollywood — one of the most powerful people in culture and business. Zoom in: The combined entity, rebranded Skydance, will house three major movie studios (Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures and Skydance), two global streamers (Paramount+ and HBO Max) and two major news networks (CNN and CBS). It will also create a cable juggernaut, marrying Paramount's Viacom channels, such as MTV, VH1 and Comedy Central, with WBD's cable networks, including TBS, TNT, Food Network and Discovery. The combination of those assets on the back end won't all be felt by consumers, but product changes are coming. The combined company, for example, plans to merge HBO Max and Paramount + into one giant unified streamer. The big picture: The transaction forced the entertainment industry and regulators around the world to confront how much consolidation is necessary for traditional media companies to compete with Big Tech. While some countries took a closer look at the deal than others, every government that required regulatory approval for the merger ultimately blessed the transaction. Although Netflix did meaningfully engage in a bidding war for WBD, it eventually abandoned its interest when the asset became too pricey. Reality check: Merger fights don't typically enter the zeitgeist for everyday Americans, but this one played into a broader societal debate around the concentration of power among the elite and the independence of federal regulators. Ellison's father, Oracle co-founder and Trump ally Larry Ellison , agreed to backstop billions of dollars of equity financing to seal the deal. Federal regulators cleared billions of dollars in equity investments from Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds to support the deal. The Federal Communications Commission, led by Trump ally Brendan Carr, granted Paramount's request to exceed foreign ownership limits for broadcasters. Between the lines: The political tension surrounding the deal was on full display when a dozen Democratic state attorneys general sued to block the transaction as it approached the finish line this summer. The state AGs said their case was rooted in traditional antitrust law around film and cable dominance, not politics. But after a settlement was announced clearing the deal, at least one participating state attorney general admitted that they wanted the agreement to force a divestiture of CBS and CNN. State of play: To alleviate regulatory concerns about the enormous concentration of assets, Skydance made a slew of commitments in its settlement, including theatrical film release minimums and investments in domestic production jobs. But the creative industry is still on edge as it anticipates a potentially huge number of job cuts as a result of the merger. What to watch: The deal, which is one of the most highly levered transactions in American history, will test the market's appetite for megamergers financed by huge amounts of debt amid rising interest rates. To get the transaction over the finish line, Paramount raised $52 billion in new debt, per Bloomberg . Some of that debt is very expensive, carrying a yield of nearly 9%. In addition to the debt it raised, Skydance will carry WBD's existing liabilities, totaling $87.5 billion in debt, according to Fitch Ratings . Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Christine Wang/Axios The bottom line: Ellison has proven himself to be one of the most savvy dealmakers in American history. His next test is whether he can build a sustainable business from a mountain of debt.

events.title: Energy forum seeks to rescue supply disrupted by US-Iran war
events.summary: Energy market insiders who gathered in a vast underground ballroom in central London this week were united in support of a new emphasis on resilience in the oil industry. The duration of the US-Iran war has changed the industry from "a just-in-time to a just-in-case" sector, TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanne told the Energy Intelligence Forum. Amin Nasser, chief executive of Aramco, said that throughout the crisis conditions, the producer has not cancelled one committed delivery, thanks to a number of routes to market and, in the case of the East-West pipeline , a vast capacity. This comes despite the supply problems caused by the blockades in the Strait of Hormuz and, more recently, the Bab Al Mandeb strait. “It [the pipeline] has multiple lines with a lot of redundancy and flexibility built in and, because of that, all our customers are getting all their shipments required,” he said. “When this crisis happened, we said, “OK, we have three routes. Is that enough?” Mr Nasser added. “Maybe not for the future. And this is the responsibility of the current generation, to think of a fourth and a fifth export way out.” Sheikh Nawaf Al Sabah, chief executive of Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC), pointed out the value of having its own tanker fleet, which dates back to the 1990s. “I think there is a major difference that we are able to accomplish through our tankers by having these tankers owned by us,” Mr Al Sabah said. “We control where they go and the crews are our own crews. They, of course, all have the discretion of deciding whether they want to go through a passage or not.” An emerging picture of new codes of conduct from the US-Iran war stretches across customers, consuming nations, producers and product classes. Vaclav Bartuška, the Czech ambassador to the UK, said the long-term forces of change bear some resemblance to calculations last seen between the US and former Soviet Union. “We are relearning the escalation ladder, which was the basis of the Cold War for 40 years,” he told The National . “You know the level to which you escalate, that you deter, but also don't cause too much pain into the other side. “The Soviet Union and the United States developed a code, a language of how to hit each other without actually having open war between them. [They] managed to spend 40 years in a Cold War without killing the world. They had proxy wars. They had plenty of conflicts. They managed not to have a direct escalation among themselves. This could be a very long confrontation. It could also end the next day,” he said. During the gas dispute between Russia and Ukraine in January 2009, Mr Bartuska was involved in negotiations with Russian, Ukrainian and European Union leadership, when the Czech Republic held the EU Presidency. He also served as the Czech Republic's ambassador-at-large for energy security. Ichiro Takahara, chairman and chief executive of Japan's strategic reserves specialist operator, Jogmec, said diversification to avoid “chokepoints” was one priority in the country's stockpiling policy. He added that relations with resilient suppliers, such as Aramco and KPC, would include co-operation to build storage depots closer to customers in places such as Japan. Another Japanese executive, Takayuki Ueda, president of Inpex, said buyers now had wider considerations concerning diversification as well as resilience. “What matters for our buyers is security of supply,” he said. “They usually point out diversification of supply sources is important. However, they also emphasise the security and resilience of entire supply chain.” Countries with differing strengths must work together to boost supply undertakings, said Kevin Gallagher, managing director of Australian company Santos. “There's a real clarity and understanding with policymakers in Australia that more pragmatic rather than ideological policies when it comes to energy development and energy supply going forward is what was required,” he said. Mr Gallagher predicted Australia would “take its foot off the hose” that has restricted oil and gas exploration in recent years. The Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led European legislators to seek new energy deals in the Gulf – but the current war has narrowed those options. Mr Bartuška said European governments were likely to pursue a diversification of suppliers. “This is not a crisis yet. We have been through much worse, and European countries didn't start this conflict and are not taking direct part in it,” he said. Rising oil and gas prices would make some previously marginal projects more economically viable. “There are quite a few projects around the world which were basically on the threshold between being relevant and not,” Mr Bartuška said. “I think higher prices will make them sustainable economically. From Latin America, from African countries and projects in Asia, Australia or the US. There are quite a few resources which are not yet reserves, or they are becoming reserves, which means economically viable, thanks to the situation now.” “I think, in general, the European perception of war changed in 2022 with the start of the Russian war against Ukraine, and we now see huge attacks by drones and missiles very regularly,” he said. “There are also plenty of hybrid or hidden warfare and hidden attacks or deniable attacks against our installations. We are much more careful about what's happening in our countries, trying to deter another attack [while at] the same time, not to escalate too much.” He said western misconception of Iran was driving the inability to reach a truce – as well as a desire from the US and Iran sides to keep the war going. “I don't know if both sides actually want the end of confrontation. I'm not sure of that. It's been going on since the end of February. It's now October,” he said.
