events.title: 'Can I be in the UAE after overstaying my visit visa?'
events.summary: Question : Can a telecoms company impose a travel ban over an unpaid bill? I owe a telecoms company money and haven't paid it for months. I have been sent a message saying that I owe Dh2,930 and that my account is now 190 days overdue. It also said: “We hereby inform you that legal proceedings may be initiated to recover the outstanding amount.” The message was from a credit management company. Can they make a case against me and put a travel ban on me for this? Is there any other action they can take? JC, Abu Dhabi Answer : For an unpaid telecom debt of Dh2,930, a full court case is unlikely, but JC can still face consequences. The account has probably already been cut off, and the company will follow up as he owes it money. Companies can pursue debts in court but, for in this case litigation costs would be disproportionate relative to the amount owed. A travel ban will not happen. Under Article 324 of the UAE Civil Procedure Law (Federal Decree Law No 42 of 2022), a creditor – a person or company that is owed money – can only apply for a travel ban against a debtor if the debt is Dh10,000 or more. Below that threshold, a civil travel ban cannot be issued, regardless of the risk of a person leaving the country without settling their debts. It is common for UAE companies to hand over small debts to collection agencies. That will lead to regular telephone calls, emails and even WhatsApp messages. These companies are licensed and regulated, and there are rules that they must follow. The agency must not overstep by making repeated calls designed to intimidate rather than to communicate, as that constitutes harassment under UAE law. They are only allowed to make contact between 9am and 8pm, and must not disclose information to any third party. That includes calling a place of work and telling anyone the call is about a debt. If the collection agency breaks these guidelines, a complaint can be made, first to the telecoms company, but if that doesn’t stop it, then to the Central Bank of the UAE. JC needs to start making repayments in order to stop follow-up calls and messages. Non-payment of any debt will affect a person’s UAE credit record . This will affect a person's ability to borrow and open financial accounts. Since the change in legislation this year, landlords can now ask for confirmation of a credit score, which can also affect a person's ability to rent a home. Q : I have overstayed my visit visa after my employer failed to arrange a work permit. What can I do? I have a question about overstaying a visit visa. I came to work for a company, and although the team promised me a visa, it never happened. I don’t have a contract, and they have now said they do not want me to work for them any more. What can I do about this? I want to find another job and stay in the UAE. Will I get in trouble or have to pay a fine? MP, Dubai A : The important point here is that MP has been working illegally since arriving in the UAE. From the outset, the employer should have given MP a proper offer of employment and a labour contract, and applied for a residence visa and a work permit. As this did not happen, the company has been employing MP illegally, so she has been working illegally. Sadly, this means that she has no protection under UAE law. This means that MP is unable to make a legal complaint against the company, even if it has broken the law. No doubt the employer will know that this is not permitted, but the company can be reported for breaking the law. Any company that takes on staff without a visa can be fined up to Dh50,000 and may have difficulty obtaining visas in the future. As MP has been in the UAE without a valid visa, MP will have overstay fines. Since February 2026, the UAE has unified overstay fines across all visa types and emirates. They are now the same for all visas, whether tourist, visit or residence visas, and there is no variation by emirate. The fine is Dh50 per day. If an overstay exceeds 30 days, an additional exit permit, known as an “outpass”, at a cost of Dh250 to Dh300, including base and service fees, is required before leaving the country. It is possible to pay the overstay fines and stay in the UAE without leaving the country, provided a new employer initiates the visa process immediately. If not, MP will need to leave and return on an employment entry permit from a new employer. MP should visit an Amer centre, a division of the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs, for advice and to find out how much MP owes. Once the overstay fine has been settled, MP can find a new job and be employed with a visa in order to stay legally in the UAE. events.title: Security researcher claims they found KVM guest-host escape flaw
events.summary: Linux KVM, the hypervisor favoured by hyperscale clouds, apparently has a full VM escape bug. That nasty news came from security researcher Paulos Yibelo, who on X shared a screenshot of a bug bounty award he won for discovering what he described as “Full VM escape zeroday (guest>host root in industry standard hypervisors)!” The bug bounty Yibelo participated in is run by Vercel, a company that provides MicroVMs as sandboxes for AI agents to work inside. The company’s Sandbox uses Firecracker MicroVMs, a technology created by AWS, which relies on Linux KVM – the kernel level hypervisor in Linux. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch named KVM as the hypervisor identified by Yibelo. “We’ve confirmed a KVM 0day through our Vercel Sandbox bounty program. Affecting the industry’s gold standard solution for Linux virtualization,” he wrote. And that’s all the info that has made it into the public view at this time. The Register can find no chat on relevant mailing lists. We have asked Rauch and Yibelo for additional details. Hopefully, we don’t hear from either of them for days or weeks, for two reasons. One is that guest-host escapes are the nightmare virtualization scenario because they mean whoever runs a guest VM could take over an entire server, and perhaps gain the ability to control other guests. The other is that KVM is astoundingly prevalent: AWS and Google both use it to power their public clouds. Enterprise virtualization players Nutanix, HPE, and Proxmox also rely on KVM. And of course KVM is also in Firecracker, which is open source and could therefore be running in all sorts of places. Whatever Yibelo discovered therefore very much needs a responsible disclosure process, because if hints about the flaw emerge it could allow attackers to do a lot of damage. Once a fix is found, the next question is whether implementing it will require disruption or downtime. It’s possible to hot-patch KVM, and to migrate live VMs from vulnerable hosts to machines running a patched version of Linux. Hopefully those techniques will work. This might be the second nasty bug discovered in KVM this year, after the so-called Januscape flaw. Beyond the potential risks this bug created, observers have suggested the potential seriousness of the flaw means Yibelo’s reward should exceed the $50,000 available under Vercel’s bug bounty program. ®

events.title: Schneider Electric drops $22.6B on PTC as datacenter boom rains money on infra companies
events.summary: Schneider Electric's market cap has more than doubled in the past four years as the AI boom has driven unprecedented demand for datacenter power and cooling infrastructure. Now the French multinational is cashing in on its good fortunes to cement its place as a key provider of industrial power and datacenter infrastructure with the $22.6 billion acquisition of American industrial software company PTC. Founded in 1985, PTC made a name for itself developing software for computer-aided design, plus lifecycle management tools for industrial products and applications. The all-cash deal, announced on Monday, positions Schneider Electric to capitalize on the proliferation of datacenters used to train and serve AI models at scale. Since ChatGPT kicked off the AI arms race in late 2022, datacenter design and power requirements have changed considerably. Forty-kilowatt air-cooled racks have given way to 250kW liquid-cooled systems that need much denser power delivery and thermal management systems, all of which need to work together. In light of the growing complexity and supply chain challenges facing datacenter deployments, Schneider has made several strategic acquisitions which expanded its role in bit barn development. In late 2024, not long after Nvidia unveiled its first all-liquid-cooled rack designs, Schneider invested roughly $850 million on a 75 percent stake in Motivair, one of the leading producers of cold plates, rack manifolds, coolant distribution units (CDUs) and rear-door heat exchangers required to support the widespread adoption of liquid-cooled servers. The company is expected to acquire the remainder of Motivair sometime in 2028. As Schneider's role in the datacenter has grown, users of its kit have more products to manage across their lifecycles. Buying PTC expands Schneider's lifecycle management offerings and introduces key design capabilities to its offerings. PTC isn't Schneider's only datacenter-centric acquisition this year. Back in June, the company paid $3.1bn for industrial data operations vendor Cognite. Speaking to investors on Monday, Schneider CEO Olivier Blum suggested that owning PTC and Cognite would enable the company to inject software-defined automation into power systems early in their development, improving their efficiency in the process. Datacenters are one of Schneider's initial targets. "We believe that at the design stage, it is super important that you can help your customer to design both product, machine, processes and energy system. This is where we see CAD engineering as a very critical part of the portfolio," Blum said, according to a transcript of his remarks to investors. That's assuming of course that Schneider doesn't run into any regulatory hurdles along the way. The deal, Schneider's largest ever, isn't expected to close until late next year. ®

events.title: Inside the transgender rights fight injecting chaos into Democrats' midterm efforts
events.summary: An intra-party debate over how best to deflect Republican attacks on transgender issues has Democrats angrily sniping at each other just weeks out from the midterm elections. Why it matters: This is not the position Democrats hoped to be in two years after their 2024 election loss , which many in the party attributed to being outflanked by GOP messaging on trans issues. "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios. "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance." "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care." Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools." "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports." Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down. One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community." What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC. He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us." Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable." What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios. The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election. "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer. "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor." Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric. Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls." That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it. The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024. "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC. Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy." Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios. "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules." "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care." The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck. Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue. Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

events.title: MCP for agent-to-agent comms may be the riskiest protocol you've never heard of
events.summary: The adoption of AI agents in millions of organizations is creating new opportunities for attackers to make them take malicious actions, such as exfiltrating database contents and sensitive business and personal information. In the past five months, Google and four other organizations—with little in common except for their use of AI agents—have acknowledged vulnerabilities that exploit one agent inside a targeted network to spread harmful instructions to other internal agents. The technique is a special form of prompt injection that targets not the LLM but a particular agent, such as one for translation or data analysis. Guardrails inside such agents, if they exist at all, are often lax and will send the instructions to other agents down the chain. Because the latter agent explicitly trusts the first one, it follows the directions. Unexpected and hard to mitigate Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents from organizations including Google, JP Morgan Chase, Weviate, Rapid7, the French government's interministerial digital directorate, and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks exploit trust gaps in MCP, short for Model Context Protocol . The standard is one way AI apps and agents communicate with each other inside an internal network. events.title: Envision to end operations and stop product development if it can't find partner
events.summary: Envision , a Netherlands-based start-up that made hardware and software tools for the visually impaired , will be stopping product development at the end of the year unless it can find a partner. In a statement posted to the company's website on Monday, founder Karthik Mahadevan and Karthik Kannan said that despite efforts towards a successful business model, the company has been unable to yield profitable results. "We reached the conclusion that we have given it our all and brought Envision as far as we could with our nimble efforts," they wrote. "There’s still so much potential for this product and business to grow, but realising it needs someone who can take it in a new direction, whether that's a new audience or a different business model." Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said they were in talks with a few possible partners who might be able to keep the company going. They were also open to speaking with others who may have ideas as to how to keep it alive. In 2024, Envision's founders spoke with The National about the company's aspirations. Its journey to selling smart glasses for the visually impaired started in 2017, when the start-up's smartphone app, Envision AI, began to gain popularity. The app uses a phone camera to identify and read signs, objects, menus, books or other material in real time, making life easier for visually impaired users. The popularity of the app's free version, according to Mr Kannan at the time, fuelled Envision's desire to improve the user experience based on feedback from customers. “If you're a low-vision person and you have to have a phone in one hand and a cane in the other, that can be cumbersome,” he said. “So we started looking for something that might be sleek and modern-looking to implement.” Part of enhancing the experience, Mr Kannan said, was to take the best aspects of the Envision app and use it in the glasses. Envision's app won a Google Play Award in 2019 in the category of “best accessibility experience”, and Mr Kannan said it could come to an agreement with Google and eventually use the company's largely defunct Google Glass technology for its product. The glasses, priced from $1,899 to $3,499, were introduced in 2020 and underwent various improvements amid the AI boom. In the announcement on Monday, the founders outlined plans to wind down operations and promised there would be a final update, with hopes of keeping the app and some offerings operational for as long as possible "offline”. Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said the ultimate problem was scaling Envision's business model to something sustainable given the competition from Apple and Meta , and the current economy. "On paper, 300 million blind and low-vision people is a big market, but for the majority of them, the problems that come first are ones technology can't solve yet: poverty, lack of basic access, unemployment," Envision’s founders wrote. "That's why even products that are cheap or free struggle to get past that million mark, and paying users are a much much smaller slice of that." In 2024, Envision told The National of the intention to turn the company's focus to Arabic . "As our user base in the Middle East grew and we built up a community of users, we've started to bring a lot more of those efforts in-house,” Mr Kannan said. “As a result, we now have more control over how the AI works when translating documents that are scanned and how it works if there's written text on a blackboard.”

events.title: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
events.summary: The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend as a result of intelligence suggesting an Iranian drone attack, U.S. officials said. Why it matters: Such an Iranian drone attack from British soil against the base could have led to the killing of U.S. service members and destroyed the strategic bombers. It would have been an unprecedented and brazen attack by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential for dramatic escalation in the war in the Middle East. When asked by reporters on Monday if Iran planned to launch a drone attack against the base from British soil, Trump said: "I can't tell you that. If they did they will suffer greatly." Driving the news: The dozen B-1 bombers were evacuated from the base in the UK only several weeks after being deployed there. The Pentagon said on Sunday that "all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States." It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States." Between the lines: The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. U.S. officials say it is unclear whether the people who were arrested are connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack. Behind the scenes: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. On Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Netanyahu from the plane on his way to Iceland, the State Department said. What they're saying: Rubio told reporters earlier that the movement of the bombers was part of "regular rotations" of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and was not directly tied to an Iranian threat. But several hours later, President Trump contradicted Rubio and told reporters the bombers were moved because of a security threat from Iran. "They didn't fly out by accident ... there was a threat. We moved them around a little bit," he said. Trump added that the U.S. knows who was behind the threat and their links to Iran. Trump was then asked about the attempted terrorist attack on the Fly Dubai flight and said he thinks Iran was responsible.

events.title: Citrix NetScaler security snafus get even worse amid more 0-day reports
events.summary: The attackers just keep coming after Citrix NetScaler appliances, as both the feds and private security researchers warn that someone found - and has already exploited - yet another Citrix bug before it had a patch. This latest vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779, is a memory overflow bug that leads to denial of service attacks. It only affects NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) service provider or identity provider, used for single sign-on authentication. Late Friday, amid exploitation reports, Citrix confirmed that it was investigating a “newly observed issue related to SAML authentication in customer-managed NetScaler deployments.” By Saturday night, the vendor released a security advisory for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway with patches, urging vulnerable customers to “install the relevant updated versions as soon as possible.” Citrix also posted a blog about the vulnerability, confirming that it has observed targeted attacks on unmitigated NetScaler deployments that can lead to denial of service. Citrix did not answer our questions about CVE-2026-88779 - including how many instances have been affected and what attackers are doing after exploiting the bug - but urged customers to "quickly apply" the fix to NetScaler instances. "We were recently alerted to a new issue that affects service availability for some NetScaler deployments," a Citrix spokesperson told The Register. "After we were alerted to this issue we immediately developed and published a mitigation while concurrently developing, testing and deploying a fix." On Sunday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed CVE-2026-88779 was under active exploitation and ordered federal agencies to patch the bug by Wednesday. While the new vulnerability is not technically related to the earlier eight CVEs finally disclosed by Citrix on September 27 - weeks after miscreants began abusing two of these security holes (CVE-2026-88772 and CVE-2026-88771) - watchTowr researchers told us they suspect it has been used to purposefully crash machines, making exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 faster. “This vulnerability is incredibly simple to trigger, with a single specially crafted request being all that is needed to knock an appliance offline,” watchTowr’s head of threat intelligence, Jake Knott, told The Register. “Exploitation is already occurring in the wild, and disrupting an authentication gateway can prevent legitimate users from accessing the services behind it.” WatchTowr reproduced the vulnerability on Friday, and Citrix credited the attack-surface management company along with Bishop Fox with helping it address the issue. “Citrix provides an indicator-of-compromise script that teams can run to check exposed appliances for signs of compromise, though a clean result is not definitive proof,” Knott said. “Security teams should prioritize appliances configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server with SAML authentication enabled, and affected organizations should apply the fixed build or Citrix’s interim mitigation if an immediate upgrade is not possible.”®

events.title: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
events.summary: President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague , though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began. Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution. Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work. No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported. What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger." The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance , but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert. The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak. Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

events.title: How states are tackling midterm pump pain
events.summary: States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections , pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled. Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs. While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution. Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief. Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing. There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders. Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March. Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days. Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters. Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so. Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels. But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns. Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries. For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities." Louisiana , Nebraska , North Carolina , Oklahoma and Texas took similar action. Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring. The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action. events.title: Cohere offers to put agents in lockdown mode with strict ACLs
events.summary: While OpenAI and Anthropic stoke fears over rogue agents, Canadian model dev Cohere promises enterprises a safer and more consistent experience. On Monday, the company said it revamped its North agent harness, which launched early last year, to improve collaboration, access control, token spend, and overall security of the platform. As you'd expect from an enterprise focused agent framework, Cohere's North 2 is designed to tie into existing knowledge bases and SaaS apps in order to automate various business processes. North 2 introduces a variety of features and functions that should be familiar to anyone who's used Claude Code or OpenClaw. Among them is the concept of skills, libraries, and automations. Skills are arguably the simplest, and are essentially standard operating procedures documenting how the agent harness should complete tasks. The skills are often generated by working with the agent to complete a task and then documenting which steps achieved the best results. With North 2, Cohere says that it has made it easier for these skills to be shared so that users aren't wasting time reinventing the wheel. Presumably, this should improve consistency by avoiding having the agent take different routes to achieving its goal, something that might miss key information or nuance. To facilitate the creation of new skills, North 2 also introduces the concept of automations, generic templates that can be customized using a drag-and-drop graphical interface, not unlike LangFlow, which we looked at earlier this year. Alongside skills and automations, Cohere's North 2 does something similar for shared knowledge and assets, which it calls libraries, to ensure that agents are working off of the same datasets. Finally, North 2 adds memory, a core feature of most modern agent harnesses, to ensure that agents can maintain context across multiple sessions. In some sense, these features are a bit like self-generating macros, but rather than being limited to Excel, they work across multiple applications and data sources. Sovereign AI remains a major talking point for Cohere, which says enterprises can deploy North 2 where they like and use their preferred models. If enterprises want to deploy the harness on-prem in an air-gapped environment, they can. If they prefer to run it in the cloud, that's also an option. Along with new features aimed at collaboration and automation, North 2 implements new guardrails designed to help enterprises get a handle on their token spend and access controls. Flow control functionality, meanwhile, promises greater visibility into which departments are hogging all the tokens, while access control functionality offers admins the ability to assign access control lists to various libraries and skills so that interns can't get their hands on proprietary data just because they asked for it. North 2 is only the latest in a slew of enterprise focused agentic AI platforms which have been rolled out over the last year. Essentially every major and minor cloud provider has introduced some kind of agent harness tailored to enterprise needs. The competition has only gotten hotter over the last few weeks as OpenAI, Meta and others have set their sights on the enterprise. ®

events.title: Get rid of Apple's AI bloatware and reclaim 12 GB of storage with this open source tool
events.summary: Apple’s attempt to integrate AI into its various operating systems hasn’t been entirely well received, nor has the decision to make Apple Intelligence increasingly difficult to disable completely. Thankfully, the open source community has come to the rescue. A recently released open source tool called RemoveMacAI does pretty much exactly what it says on the GitHub-hosted tin: Aggressively rips Apple Intelligence out of macOS, disabling most of its AI features and removing downloaded models following the launch of macOS 27 last month. Siri AI? Gone. ChatGPT and other AI extensions? Eliminated. Genmoji, random boxes offering to jazz up your writing, summaries of notifications and app content, and automatic photo clean-up? Never to be seen again. More importantly, RemoveMacAI can claw back the storage occupied by Apple’s AI models - potentially over 12 GB, depending on the Mac. You might just get confused and think it’s 2025 again. The impetus for RemoveMacAI, its creator Om Lahorey said in a LinkedIn post, is the fact that Apple made it practically impossible to remove Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27. “The settings are spread across about a dozen places, some of them only under Screen Time,” Lahorey wrote over the weekend. “Even with every one turned off, the models stay on disk. I wanted it gone in one step, so I wrote RemoveMacAI.” Unsurprisingly, Lahorey’s tool blew up on Hacker News, with plenty of people happy for an easy way to get rid of Apple AI tools. As of writing, the repo has over 1,500 stars, so it's clearly struck a nerve with frustrated macOS users. It’s simple to run, as its GitHub page explains: install it via a curl command to its GitHub repo, or with Homebrew, and then fire it up in the terminal. Selected features can be left enabled, or Apple Intelligence can be disabled completely, while a single command can revert the changes and restore the previous settings. RemoveMacAI works by installing a configuration profile, which the user has to approve, that applies Apple’s own restriction keys for Apple Intelligence features. Models are then removed via Apple’s asset service. Lahorey credits another open source tool called pared, and its developer, with mapping the asset service, model sets, and settings keys needed to remove Apple Intelligence. Pared functions similarly to RemoveMacAI – you can consider RemoveMacAI to be a more user-friendly wrapper for the other tool. As for whether it will persist, Lahorey explains that the config profile RemoveMacAI installs redirects the download for Apple Intelligence models to a closed local port, so updates to macOS shouldn’t result in the models being reinstalled. Also worth mentioning, Apple System Integrity Protection remains enabled with the models disabled and uninstalled, as no files under System are directly modified by the tool. Dictation should still work as well, as speech models aren’t removed by RemoveMacAI. That said, it’s certainly possible a future macOS update will break RemoveMacAI’s functionality. So if you’re interested in giving the tool a shot, there’s no guarantee this particular escape hatch will remain open forever. ®

events.title: Backside Clock Meshes Cut Skew and Power in 2nm Nanosheets (UCSC)
events.summary: Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz published a technical paper titled “Design Space Exploration of Backside Clock Meshes for 2 nm GAAFET BSPDN Technology.” Abstract Excerpt: “Clock meshes are used in high-performance VLSI designs to minimize skew and tolerate on-chip variation, but they spend scarce routing resources on premium metal layers. Backside power delivery creates a new option: it adds thick, low-resistance metal layers on the back of the wafer, and the power grid does not consume all of them. Flip-flops remain on the frontside; a backside mesh therefore cannot drive them directly, and every connection passes through a through-silicon via. We present the first design-space exploration of backside clock meshes, implemented in OpenROAD on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology.” Find the technical paper here. October 2026. events.title: 6 Guidelines for Governing AI
events.summary: For the first 10 years of my career, I worked in product management and data analytics by myself. I wrote database queries that pulled numbers out of corporate systems, built statistical models to predict what customers would buy, and shipped data pipelines that moved information between business systems. I built and scaled analytics teams at Best Buy and Target , studying how customers shop and what stores should stock. Today I lead enterprise AI transformation at Lowe’s , the Fortune 100 home improvement retailer. The goal is not to sell artificial intelligence ; it is to use it to deliver useful expertise at the moment a customer needs it. In retail and other customer-facing industries, virtual assistants can help people address everyday questions—such as how to repair a leaky faucet—while guiding them toward relevant products, services, or next steps. As these capabilities become more common, technology roles are changing. The work is no longer limited to building AI systems ; it also includes defining how they operate: which decisions they can make autonomously, when they must escalate to a person, and which actions must remain off-limits. That shift—from building AI systems to governing them —is coming for anyone who is accountable for what such systems produce. Not the casual user typing into a chatbot but the engineers, product managers, analysts, and business operators who sign off on work a machine drafted. It is the subject of the book I recently coauthored, The Enterprise Brain . I call the change the “governor shift,” from executing tasks yourself to setting the intent, principles, and boundaries within systems that execute them for you. Business operators might not write code; they will decide which pricing exceptions an agent may approve and which it must escalate. That is governing. A 2025 report from MIT Media Lab’s Project NANDA found that, despite an estimated US $30 billion to $40 billion in enterprise generative-AI investment, the vast majority of organizations in its dataset had not yet demonstrated measurable profit-and-loss impact. The report estimated that only about 5 percent of integrated pilots were generating substantial value, underscoring how difficult it remains to move from experimentation to scaled business outcomes. Researchers named the pattern the GenAI Divide , the term I adopted for the book. The companies rarely lack technology; they use the same models as the 5 percent that are winners. But they lack people who can direct the systems and stand behind the results. Guidelines to follow Here are six guidelines. Recognize when you have become “human middleware.” In software, “middleware” is the code that sits between two systems and passes information back and forth. Many of us have become its human version. Take an honest look at your week. How much time is spent pulling data out of one tool, reformatting it, and routing it to another team? I call this the “administrator trap,” which is set by the architecture, not by the people caught in it. Relaying is what AI agents now do well. But they cannot judge which numbers deserve attention, which risks are real, or which compromises are worth making. Trade rules for principles. For many years, workers used rules to manage their work. Refunds for a product over a certain amount needed a signature from upper management, for example. Writing code needed two reviewers. Rules work at human speed. But rules break when a system makes thousands of decisions per hour and meets situations no rulebook anticipated, such as a complaint covered by three different policies. A rule says to do exactly this specific thing; a principle says to achieve the outcome without crossing certain lines. Governing AI means writing those principles in priority order so the system settles its own conflicts the way a well-led team does when the manager is not available. Never harm the customer. Tell the truth even if the company loses a sale. Protect the economics, and then move quickly. Underneath sits a question of decision rights: the formal authority over who or what may make a given call. Writing down the answers in what I call a “library of principles” is now core leadership work, whether you’re a technologist or a business owner. Write your culture into your code. Many companies have turned their values into posters that hang on office walls. But an AI agent cannot read the posters. Instead, write your governance as code. Include your values and policies as machine-readable instructions that the AI agent will follow automatically. Do so in three layers. The top is the constitution, which states the rules an agent may never break, and never state a fact it cannot support. The second layer is the doctrine: how the business competes and the acceptable trade-offs to get there, such as protecting a long-term relationship over a short-term sale. At the bottom sits the playbook, which has the tactics used for one task. Install a trust thermostat, not a trust switch. The question that stalls nearly every company’s AI deployment is some version of: “What if it tells our biggest customer something wrong, or quotes a price we will not honor?” It might. Treating trust as a switch leaves two bad options: an unsupervised system or a human reviewing every transaction—which would cost more than the automation would save. The alternative is a thermostat. Every decision an agent makes carries a confidence score measured against the principles set. Above an agreed threshold, it proceeds alone; below it, a human decides. That person’s answer is fed back into the learning loop so the next similar case clears the threshold on its own. Every decision stays transparent, auditable, and explainable—which is what I call a glass box. Fix context before you govern. You cannot govern a system that cannot see the whole picture. Ask your best employee about a project, and they will pull together the budget, the contract clause, and the customer’s last complaint because they know it all by heart. Most enterprise AI fails that test, because the information sits scattered across applications that store it in incompatible formats. I describe the full loop as Connections, Context, Reasoning, Actions, and Governance (CCRAG). Connections feed in raw information such as transactions and service records. Context weaves it into a context graph, which is a single connected picture of the business that gives agents something close to memory. Reasoning makes the decisions. Actions carry them back into the business systems. Governance keeps things aligned with the company’s intent. Most organizations obsess over the reasoning in the middle and underinvest in context and governance, which is exactly where humans play a role. Context compounds: Every interaction makes the graph richer and harder to reproduce. Learn to lead by exception. The most important change in habit comes last. events.title: FBI confirms 'multiple' arrests related to ShinyHunters hack
events.summary: The FBI and law enforcement partners have arrested “multiple” suspects as part of an investigation into a September hack allegedly involving data-theft-and-extortion group ShinyHunters, the bureau told The Register. “The bureau continues to aggressively investigate the recent cyber incident allegedly involving ShinyHunters, having already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects and we will spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice,” an FBI spokesperson told us in an email on Monday. The FBI declined to comment on the specific arrests, including that of Saif al-Din Khader, a suspected ShinyHunters member who has reportedly been detained in Jordan, according to Reuters. Khader, who goes by the alias Rey, was reportedly brought into custody on September 29, and is said to be cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the group. ShinyHunters did not respond to The Register’s inquiries about the arrest and Khader’s alleged involvement with the criminal group. Rey confirmed his real identity - Khader - to security journalist Brian Krebs last year. Krebs described Khader as the “technical operator and public face” of Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. “Rey got picked up finally,” said security sleuth Kevin Beaumont following news of the arrest. According to Beaumont, Rey was “one of the kids who got into JLR.” The Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which occurred in late August 2025, affected the company's IT systems and halted manufacturing operations. Dealer systems also went down, and suppliers faced canceled or delayed orders. In addition to crippling the carmaker’s business operations for months, the digital thieves stole personal payroll data belonging to thousands of JLR employees. The cyberattack, one of the most costly in UK history, was attributed to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. Khader’s detention came two weeks after the Dutch National Police arrested a 24-year-old whom the FBI described as “one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters.” While Dutch cops have not named the suspect, Krebs and other reports say he is Pepijn van der Stap, who was convicted in 2023 for hacking and extorting numerous organizations and was on supervised release after three years in prison. Van der Stap also worked as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian and volunteered as a security researcher at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). In a video message following the arrest, Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, had some advice for the “remaining members” of the data theft and extortion gang. “Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk, and seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who's left,” Leatherman said last week. “The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us, and we know how to find you. I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours.” At the time, the FBI declined to answer The Register’s questions about the video message, including whether it had seized any of the cybercrime group’s infrastructure, and whether any of ShinyHunters’ members had taken Leatherman up on his offer to “reach out first.” In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBIJobs.gov portal and claimed it stole sensitive personal details about current, former, and prospective FBI employees. A spokesperson told The Register that unlike most of its digital break-ins, this one was “NOT financially motivated … We want the FBI to correct or retract their statements they made, which included substantial false allegations.” Later, in an exclusive interview, the spokesperson told us the attention-grabbing hack was “fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.” ®

events.title: Windows 11 26H2 blighted by new audio issue
events.summary: Microsoft Windows 11 26H2 has arrived, and, unfortunately, it's already picked up a known audio issue within weeks of release. The glitch also affects Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2, which share the same code branch. It relates to decoding AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio and can cause the application using the decoder to crash abruptly or fail to start at all. Identified after the September 22 Windows update, the issue mostly impacts older applications, according to Microsoft. "Many modern applications do not use Windows for this type of encoding and therefore will not encounter this issue. "The code component involved in this issue is most commonly used in legacy applications that still rely on Windows built-in audio decoding." In summary – if your app has the temerity to use Windows built-in audio decoding for AC-3, you might have a problem. If it includes its own audio decoding component, you should be okay. "Affected applications may vary," explained Microsoft, "and can include games, media players, and certain productivity applications." There's also no fix as yet, so uninstalling is the only way to address it for now. To be clear, the AC-3 malfunction is not specific to Windows 11 26H2; the update preceded the release of the operating system's latest version by a week. It joins other known issues in 26H2, including other ongoing audio woes that have lingered in the list despite workarounds being available from Microsoft Support for Business. Microsoft currently has no mitigation for the AC-3 bug and offers little comfort to affected users: "We are working on releasing a resolution for this issue in a future Windows update." Acknowledging the latest trouble continues a run of misfortune for Microsoft. September's Patch Tuesday resulted in an out-of-band update to deal with RDP and Hyper-V issues. The update did not, however, fix all the audio problems it introduced, and the September 22 preview update has compounded the situation. Microsoft did not provide a timeline for resolving the latest issue. ®

events.title: House GOP whip: Limit spending to districts with "biggest return"
events.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is scaling back expectations and zeroing in on a narrowed battlefield as Republicans' prospects of keeping their majority look increasingly bleak. Why it matters: Emmer, a former National Republican Congressional Committee chair who helped the GOP unexpectedly gain seats in 2020, argues his party can still defy historical headwinds in November. But with less than a month to go, Emmer acknowledges that some tough decisions are coming about where Republicans spend their money, including walking away from races they don't think they can salvage. "It really is a business, and you're looking at a balance sheet, and you're putting your money where you're gonna get your biggest return," he told Axios aboard a plane between campaign stops. Axios joined Emmer, who plans to visit 56 districts between September and Election Day, as he traveled from Charlotte to Richmond last week for stops with Reps. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.). Driving the news: It's a lesson Emmer says Republicans learned the hard way in 2022, when expectations of a "red wave" led the party to spread its resources too broadly. "We expanded the map when we should have kept it narrow," Emmer told donors in Charlotte. "We should have been conservative about what we were going after." This cycle, Emmer said Republicans have to identify "where you're not gonna be able to salvage this, and you've got to pick up something over there." Yes, but : That strategy is being tested by a difficult national environment for Republicans, with an unpopular president and voters focused on the cost of living and the war in Iran, which is driving up gas prices. Between the lines: Asked about embattled Rep. Max Miller's (R-Ohio) increasingly difficult race , Emmer immediately pointed up the ticket to the Senate and gubernatorial races, where Democrats are faring better than expected. "The problem is, when you got these statewide candidates that are not creating momentum, that's tough," he said. Emmer also pointed to the North Carolina Senate race, where Democrat Roy Cooper has opened up a lead in polls, as having a "large impact" on the 1st and 11th district races there. Miller has a path to victory, Emmer said, "but it's narrow." Still, he defended the NRCC's decision to spend money backing Miller. Zoom in: Emmer's instinct is to let members run the race that fits their district — within limits. He called Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar's (R-Fla.) campaign ad breaking with Trump on immigration a "huge mistake," adding, "I'm not sure why now was the time for that message" (although he later walked back those comments, saying Salazar "knows her district"). Salazar posited in the ad that Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have "gone too far" and that Hispanic voters who helped elect him in 2024 "feel betrayed."

events.title: Altman-backed Volantis reveals plan to vault the memory wall by baking photonics into AI accelerators
events.summary: Sam Altman-backed AI chip startup Volantis has a plan to break through the memory wall using light, and this time it's not just an IP play. Founded in 2022, the San Francisco-based startup is developing an AI accelerator that will use a photonic interposer to dramatically increase memory bandwidth without compromising on capacity. Volantis believes it can pack upwards of 10 TB of memory at speeds up to 240 TB/s onto a single massive package. This, it claims, should be enough to serve a 20 trillion parameter model at 10,000 tok/s per user. To do this, Volantis is taking a somewhat unusual approach. Rather than developing some novel compute architecture or memory technology, the company is focusing its efforts on the optical interposer. Everything else it plans to license from IP providers. "The differentiation is primarily coming from the optical interposer. So why don't we license absolutely everything we possibly can, even if it's not the highest performance in the world, because we're already biting off a lot of risk with the interposer and the integration," CEO Tapa Ghosh tells El Reg. The basic idea behind the chip, which Volantis is calling A-1, is that by using optical wave guides rather than electrical interconnects it can dramatically increase the amount of high-bandwidth memory per package. Because of the speeds at which most AI accelerator memory, like HBM, operate, and the size and number of data pins used, it needs to be as close to the compute as possible to minimize power consumption and maximize signal integrity. As a result the maximum capacity and bandwidth of modern GPUs is limited by the compute die's shoreline. That's the physical perimeter around the chip. For now, that means the cap is right around 432 GB on AMD's MI455X. Photonic interconnects can extend that much farther. Instead of a few millimeters the memory can be located a few centimeters away, eliminating the shoreline as a bottleneck. While HBM is useful as an example, we'll note Volantis hasn't said what memory tech its chip will use just yet. Volantis aims to achieve this using optical waveguides integrated into an interposer. Compute and memory designed or supplied by its partners will be packaged on top. If any of this sounds familiar, Volantis isn't the first to propose using silicon photonic interposers in this manner. As our sister site Next Platform has previously reported, both Lightmatter and Celestial AI have toyed with the idea in the past. In fact, we strongly suspect the idea of HBM-at-a-distance contributed to Marvell's decision to acquire Celestial for $5.5 billion. However, unlike either Celestial or Lightmatter, Volantis isn't trying to license its tech to other chipmakers. At least not yet. Instead it aims to develop a fully fledged inference chip. "It is, at least on day one, a way easier problem to demonstrate a solution that ships," Ghosh says. Another differentiator is the technology on which the startup's interposer is based. Rather than relying on external lasers, Volantis' design uses micro vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers — micro-VCSELs for short — and means the light source is integrated directly into the interposer. VCSELs aren't new by any means, but have faced criticism over their reliability. However, Volantis CTO Roy Meade tells us the technology has come a long way in recent years and by giving up some speed, significantly higher reliability can be achieved, a philosophy he describes as wide and efficient. "People are still constrained to this, what I would call a fat pipe point-to-point mentality, and naturally, if that's the case, you're going to go towards SerDes," he says. "If we were to go back and take a look at the benefits of a wide-and-efficient approach. HBM for example. Taking that same playbook makes a lot of sense." What Meade is getting at is that interconnects can achieve higher bandwidth in a couple different ways. The first is by increasing the link speed, and the second by using more links. For example an 800 Gbps link can be achieved using four 200 Gbps links or eight 100 Gbps links. In his example of HBM, higher bandwidth is achieved by using an extremely-wide bus but slower data rate per pin relative to other memory technologies. The same concept applies to Volantis' optical interposer-based accelerator. Power efficiency remains an open question that's dogged many photonics startups, but this may be less of a problem for Volantis because it's not trying to license its first-gen interposer tech. For its first product the company is targeting 1 picojoule per bit per 24 Gbps lane and a total system power of around 20kW. Volantis still has a ways to go before it tapes out its first production-ready chip, and will need to raise a fair bit more in venture capital to do that — far more than the $88 million it raised this week with the help of Lachy Groom, Abstract Ventures, and others. Ghosh is well aware of this. He says the funding will enable the company to scale from small-scale optical demonstrators to something more closely resembling the final product. The interposer alone is challenging enough, but then there is the complexity of actually integrating the IP they license. "Aggressively, we should aim for an MVP product in 12 to 18 months as our target," he tells us, noting that's to have a working prototype not volume production. ®

events.title: Row-Parallel DRAM Computing Cuts Data-Reorganization Overhead (Syracuse, FAU, TU Dresden)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Syracuse University, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg , and TU Dresden published a technical paper titled “RAPID: Row-Parallel Arithmetic Processing in DRAM.” Abstract Excerpt: “Processing-using-memory (PUM) architectures perform computation directly within DRAM to reduce costly data movement between memory and processors. Because charge-sharing operations are confined to individual bitlines, existing DRAM-PUM architectures reorganize data into column-oriented, bit-serial representations. This organization is fundamentally incompatible with the row-oriented, word-parallel layouts used by conventional processors and accelerators, requiring expensive data-layout transformations whenever computation transitions between PUM and conventional execution. In this paper, we present RAPID, a Row-parallel Arithmetic Processing-In-DRAM architecture. RAPID augments the DRAM subarray with two lightweight extensions: migration cells that enable localized horizontal data movement between neighboring bitlines and inversion cells that provide efficient in-array logical inversion. These primitives enable RAPID to operate directly on row-parallel, bit-parallel data, preserving CPU-compatible layouts while exploiting the massive parallelism of the DRAM subarray.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Eurodrama in currency markets raises U.S. dollar's standing
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on Monday as political and fiscal worries rattled European markets. Why it matters: Rising borrowing costs and political instability are reviving concerns about strains within the eurozone — and whether the European Central Bank may eventually have to step in. France is grappling with high deficits, rising long-term rates and political stalemate over how to address them, as our colleague Emily Peck noted . Spain's prime minister called a snap election for Nov. 29, which could strengthen Pedro Sánchez's position or open the door to a populist right government. By the numbers: The euro fell below $1.12, its lowest since May 2025 and down about 4% since Sept. 8. Between the lines: France's rising borrowing costs echo the eurozone crisis of the early 2010s, though the ECB now has more tools to contain market stress. What they're saying: In an opinion article Monday in the Financial Times, former ECB board member Lorenzo Bini Smaghi called for the central bank to suspend its quantitative tightening program in light of stress on long-term rates. Compared with the early 2010s, the ECB "is much better equipped to address tensions in financial markets that could endanger the integrity of the single currency," he wrote. "It has bond-buying tools and programmes that address spikes in yields." "However, one aspect that is more difficult to understand for observers and market participants is why, in the current stress, the ECB continues to implement its policy of quantitative tightening," he continues, or shrinking its balance sheet by not replacing government bonds as they mature. "This policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure," Bini Smaghi wrote.

events.title: Dennis Hastert, disgraced ex-House speaker, dies at 84
events.summary: Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican House speaker in U.S. history who later admitted to sexually abusing several teenage boys, died Saturday at 84. The big picture: Hastert was the highest-ranking elected official in U.S. history to serve time in federal prison, and Congress still conducts business under an unwritten rule named after him. Driving the news: Hastert died at his home in Plano, Illinois, while under hospice care, the Kendall County Coroner's Office told Axios in an emailed statement. He is survived by his wife, Jean Kahl, and their two sons. Catch up quick: Hastert pleaded guilty to evading banking laws in 2015 after prosecutors investigated him for concealing large cash withdrawals. Court proceedings revealed he paid hush money to cover up his past sexual abuse of boys while working as a teacher and high school wrestling coach. Prosecutors alleged that Hastert molested at least four boys, some as young as 14. He faced no sexual abuse charges due to the statute of limitations. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison and released in 2017 after serving 13 months. Zoom out: While in Congress, Hastert became known for the unwritten Hastert Rule, under which the speaker will only bring a bill to the floor for a vote if a majority of the majority party supports it. Critics say the rule encouraged partisanship by keeping bipartisan bills off the floor if they lack support from most members of the majority party. Early life Hastert was born in Aurora, Kane County, Illinois, on Jan. 2, 1942. He attended Wheaton College and earned a master's degree from Northern Illinois University. He later worked as a high school teacher and athletic coach at Yorkville High School, where the abuse of at least four athletes took place. He left education for politics, winning a seat in the Illinois House of Representatives, where he served from 1980 to 1986. Hastert then won election to the U.S. House, serving from 1987 to 2007. Professional career Hastert has been dubbed the "accidental speaker" after he won the gavel in 1999 as a compromise candidate after Newt Gingrich resigned and the expected replacement, Bob Livingston , withdrew. Hastert led the House during the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks and for most of President George W. Bush's administration. After his resignation , he became a highly paid lobbyist until his indictment. The indictment Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to one count of illegally structuring cash withdrawals to evade federal reporting requirements. His plea agreement says Hastert paid an unnamed individual $1.7 million between 2010 and 2014 after the person confronted him about "past misconduct" Hastert committed against them decades earlier. Hastert had agreed to pay the individual $3.5 million to resolve the matter. From 2010 to 2012, he regularly withdrew roughly $50,000 in cash every six weeks to make the payments. After bank representatives questioned him about the large withdrawals, Hastert began taking out less than $10,000 at a time to evade federal reporting requirements. He ultimately withdrew $952,000 in those smaller increments. Hastert later stopped making payments before reaching the agreed-upon $3.5 million, prompting the individual to sue him for the remaining money. That lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court. After the indictment Hastert's state pensions from working as a teacher and in the state legislature were forfeited and revoked in the years after his indictment. His federal pension, worth more than $70,000 a year, was still in place. His name was also removed from Wheaton University's Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy in 2015, and his official House Speaker portrait was removed from the Speaker's Lobby. events.title: Trump's economic tightrope messaging of strong economy, high prices
events.summary: President Trump's economic officials acknowledge that a strong economy alone will not persuade Americans that they are better off under this president. Why it matters: The administration is trying to avoid what it sees as a Biden-era mistake: touting strong economic data while Americans are still reeling from a historic run-up in prices to which Trump's policies have contributed. It is a high-wire messaging act just weeks before the midterms: The administration wants to promote strong growth without appearing to dismiss Americans' frustration over the cost of living. "If I say, 'Oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," top White House economist Kevin Hassett said on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday. What they're saying: "What we're not going to do is do what the Biden people did and tell the American people how good they had it," Bessent told Axios' Mike Allen on Friday in a wide-ranging interview on "The Axios Show." Bessent said that the economy remains strong despite the recent inflation surge. "Any of the numbers are quite strong, other than headline inflation," which includes energy prices driven up by the Middle East conflict. He predicted the energy shock would "fade away." He acknowledged that Americans are still dealing with the cumulative hit from higher prices: "Sometimes I feel like an emergency room doctor. ... The American people were backed over by the inflation Mack Truck." The Treasury secretary said that wages keeping pace with inflation now isn't enough to make up for the earlier erosion in purchasing power. "Breaking even after what happened during the Biden years is not our goal." Yes, but: The administration still wants credit for the strong economy on paper, even as the headline economic indicators obscure the financial strain Americans still feel. "There is the stated preference and revealed preference," Bessent said, referring to Americans' spending behavior versus their weak sentiment. The other side: "What we did was to say, 'hey, we know you're struggling and we're trying to help with prices, but look at this good GDP or jobs report!' That talked past people," Jared Bernstein, former White House top economist under Biden, told Axios in an email. "What they mostly say is 'You're not struggling! And the economy's booming.' That too talks past people." Bernstein argued that the administration has not only dismissed affordability concerns — Trump called the affordability crisis a "hoax" last year — but worsened them through tariffs, budget cuts and the war. The big picture: The bond market is complicating the administration's affordability push as long-term interest rates rise sharply and mortgage rates top 7%. Bessent has made lower Treasury yields a pillar of the administration's affordability push. A speech he gave last year had one section titled "Treasury Markets as a Barometer for Affordability." Speaking to Axios, Bessent played down the signal from the recent yield surge, pointing out that borrowing costs have climbed around the world. "I would be concerned if we were having some kind of idiosyncratic rise," he said. "It's been a global rise." What to watch: The Treasury secretary recognized the limits of his influence on the bond market after this summer's intervention . "I can't control the bond market," he said. "What I can do is try to get people to slow down and think." Bessent said he does not regret declaring last month that "I am the house now," a reference to his informational advantage over Wall Street. "The house doesn't win every hand. The house plays percentages." Go deeper: Watch the extended Scott Bessent interview on "The Axios Show"

events.title: The Iran war is hitting America's school buses — and kids are paying the price
events.summary: For millions of children, the school day starts on a diesel-powered bus with a driver behind the wheel. Now, school districts are struggling to afford both. Why it matters: The Iran War is sending diesel costs higher just as districts are grappling with a yearslong bus driver shortage — a double whammy that can ripple into missed breakfasts, late classes and fewer school activities. What they're saying: "We're a non-instructional expense for a district," Peter Mannella of the National Association for Pupil Transportation tells Axios. "The inclination is always going to be let's see what we can cut out of transportation costs because we don't want to affect the school library," he says, adding that districts would rather protect spending on teachers, aides, and special education. The big picture: Districts are consolidating routes, cutting trips and squeezing more efficiency out of their fleets. A May survey of 188 school officials found 40% had adjusted routes, 27% enforced anti-idling rules, 25% cut routes, 20% limited optional trips, 14% changed fuel purchasing and 8% made students walk farther to stops. Mannella said those changes result in more parents driving students to school activities or districts moving pickup points farther from students' homes. "It starts to affect kids and families, which you know you'd rather not do," he said. Case in point: Cherry Creek Public Schools outside Denver is short about 40 drivers, transportation director Mark Ingram tells Axios. "It's an all hands on deck thing," he said. "Every morning and afternoon, we're looking at running some routes 10 to 15 minutes late … we just don't have the people to cover the routes." For some students, that can mean missing the school-provided breakfast or arriving late to first period, he said. Ingram's district has about 611 vehicles, including 320 yellow buses, plus vehicles for students with special needs and other district operations. The district budgeted $1.5 million for fuel this year, up $300,000. It now expects to spend roughly $2 million to $2.3 million. Ingram said the district hasn't cut services but is being frugal. Zoom in: The driver shortage isn't just about wages. Nick Martini, a former school bus driver who is now an executive at a Minneapolis-area school bus contractor, said drivers must simultaneously manage children and traffic while meeting extensive training, licensing and safety requirements. Split shifts can keep drivers tied up for 10 to 12 hours while paying for only a fraction of that time, and districts compete with delivery and logistics companies for the same workers with commercial-driver's licenses . Between the lines: Rural districts have even fewer escape routes. Whereas kids in urban and suburban areas can sometimes walk to school, rural children may live miles from school, requiring longer bus routes, while districts struggle to match private-sector driver pay or hire third-party operators. Special-needs transportation can be similarly expensive because curb-to-curb routes may have long gaps between stops. Flashback: The Biden administration offered federal funding to electrify school bus fleets, but some of those programs have since slowed or ended, Association of School Business Officials International's Elleka Yost tells Axios. Electric buses aren't an immediate fix everywhere. Yost pointed to narrow or winding roads, small bridges, extreme temperatures and a lack of trained technicians. The bottom line: Districts will keep adapting, Mannella said. "We are inherently problem solvers," he said. "Transportation is too important to just let us say, 'Well, we're not going to be able to do that anymore.' We'll find a way." Go deeper: School bus tech drives classroom gains

events.title: OpenAI to flood your eyeballs with visual ads
events.summary: After adding text-based ads to its chatbot earlier this year, OpenAI announced on Monday that it was adding a new “visual ad format” to ChatGPT, which is precisely what it sounds like: Visual ads, like so much of the advertising content online, will now be part of the ChatGPT experience. OpenAI will initially test these ads during image generation. “Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy,” OpenAI explained. “For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.” If you build it, someone in the ‘States will inevitably find a way to cram an ad into it, which is why testing of OpenAI’s new ad format will begin sometime in October in the US, given its status as the advertising hellscape capital of the world. Visual ChatGPT ads will be initially tested during image generation in ChatGPT, though like much of the scheme it’s not particularly clear how that’ll work from OpenAI’s announcement. The company didn’t detail much of anything about the process, so ads might appear as a de facto loading screen while ChatGPT conjures up whatever visual slop users ask of it, or they might remain on screen after the image is generated. Or not - OpenAI told us it would have more to share once the ads enter testing. It’s also entirely unclear whether the ads will be generated by ChatGPT on the fly or pulled from a library of ads submitted by companies. OpenAI also didn’t say how it will target visual ads, which has one advertising firm CEO questioning whether the new format will be worth the expense for companies looking for captive eyeballs. "Search ads work because they meet people at the moment they're looking for something,” Donatas Smailys, CEO of creator marketing firm Billo, told The Register in an email. “Someone generating an image in ChatGPT is not shopping." OpenAI has explained how it matches ads to ChatGPT conversations, Smailys added, but given it hasn’t mentioned how it plans to target visual ads, he remains unconvinced that they’ll be an effective advertising tool. That, and they’ll be intrusive - it’s bad enough getting targeted text ads or being invited to chat with an advertising AI after clicking an ad - now visual clutter will be part of ChatGPT, too. Free users can opt out of ads without paying, but doing so disables tools including image generation; if you want to generate images without ads, Plus starts at $20 a month. ®
